in writing. a flagrant admission of the european union's impotence, reduced to asking the turkish president to respect the agreement on the control of migrants, which will have cost some six billion euros. this is in addition to the €3.2 billion received since 2014 under the instrument for pre-accession assistance. a generosity that does not prevent the turkish president from having a high-pitched and acerbic speech. this is evidenced by his undignified remarks, in which he flatly equated the greek government with the hitler regime. such disregard will not be surprising, however, when the european union does not even have the decency to show solidarity with its own member states. i am referring in particular to commissioner ylva johansson, who preferred to point the finger at the greek authorities rather than advocate the emergency border measures permitted by article 78 (3) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, which are now as obvious as they are urgent. this crisis will have served as a warning. because, like viktor orban, only leaders with a strong sense of nationalism will have been able to take the tough decisions: those that involve reconnecting with national borders, and to put it simply, with common sense.
in writing. the greek border situation has shown where things can go when politicians sweep problems under the carpet. migration and border protection was exactly such an issue. european leaders didn't want to deal with it, so they gave turkey the task of guarding europe's gates with the 2016 agreement. the hungarian government was the only one in 2015 to stand up for the protection of the borders, even at the cost of facing unfounded criticism and a brutal attack. european leaders seem to have finally understood the importance of border protection and security in order to preserve the much-vaunted european freedoms, values and way of life. better late than never. nevertheless, the hungarian people's party delegation fully supports the greek government's steps to protect the border.
in writing. this is not another debate on immigration, nor a solidarity speech contest. we greeks have taken on a huge responsibility that no country can bear alone. we have a hybrid war on europe's borders with the turkish authorities arming the migrant population without respect for human rights. we are politicians to give solutions immediately! we must demand that the dublin reform be passed by the council, that frontex be sent to turkey, that european embassies in turkey be opened for asylum applications so that there are legal pathways for trapped refugees, thus keeping the eu's borders secure with respect for human rights. the more we are absent from developments in our neighbourhood, the more we will give way to nationalist, populist and extremist interests. and no, it is not enough for europe to open its wallet to shift its responsibilities. we need to get to the root of the problem! common and european!
in writing. there was hope that the migration crisis would end in 2016 with the signing of an agreement between the european union and turkey. it was premature optimism. a new wave of migrants and a repeat of the 2015-2016 migration crisis can be expected. it is time for a pragmatic, holistic approach to migration, both internally and externally. first, it is essential that the relevant eu agencies support the efforts of member states currently under migration pressure to strengthen border security and combat human trafficking groups. until recently, greece was condemned for its tough stance on migrants at its borders, and is now called the shield of europe. today, european politicians are coming to greece in an act of solidarity. it's good that the eu elites have changed their minds, because until recently, they were calling for solidarity in accepting migrants. too bad it's too soon, when there's already been a security breach. secondly, cooperation with turkey must remain a key element of european policy. it is necessary to maintain the commitments towards turkey under that agreement. the union's macro-financial assistance should be directed to the union's macro-financial assistance to the countries of central and eastern europe, the associated countries cyprus, malta and turkey, and to the countries of the western balkans, the associated countries cyprus, malta and turkey. why is cooperation with turkey a problem for representatives of the liberal-left ideology? the lack of cooperation and support for turkey is against the interests of the whole union. it's time to learn from the past.
in writing. the external borders of the union are the borders of all and all member states must stand in solidarity with the greek government. the erdogan government is using human lives to put pressure on the union. the coordinated action of the three presidents and their visit to the greek-turkish border have clearly demonstrated the determination of the union to have a common response to the migratory pressure brought about by the erdogan government. as vice-president of the intergroup on the rights of the child in the european parliament, i cannot fail to draw attention to the worrying situation of unaccompanied children at our borders. there are over 5,000 unaccompanied children in hotspots and many lack access to their most basic rights, such as shelter, water, food, medical and psychological care. i share the greek government's concern about their situation and i join its call for support from the other eu member states to voluntarily relocate unaccompanied children. we are still short of a medium-term pact for the common management of migration and asylum. this is a priority for the president of the commission, and i fully support her.
in writing. the european union is aware of turkey's efforts to host and feed syrian refugees and has therefore been providing enormous support to the country since 2016. the european union must not, however, allow itself to be put under pressure. the people who are fleeing must not be the pawns of geopolitical interests. the crucial point is that we need humanity and order on the turkish-greek border. both are missing at the moment. a situation like 2015 cannot happen again. this means above all one thing: no uncontrolled migration to europe. in order to ensure order, we must ensure effective protection of the eu's external borders. the events of the past few weeks have shown that the european union must be stronger, more united and more strategic in its thinking, its actions and its external communication. it is high time for the eu to find a humane, effective and comprehensive approach to migration. it is extremely important that commission president ursula von der leyen has resumed the dialogue with the turkish president. the aim must be to organise, control and reduce migration.
in writing. the situation on the greek-turkish border is critical. but let us not forget that this is first and foremost the european union's border, where thousands of migrants are wandering and where human rights are being violated. they became hostages to geopolitical maneuvers. we're talking about greece needing real support. i agree with you. but this is not about the eu's millions of euros to strengthen its borders, but about creating humanitarian corridors and a mechanism for relocation and childcare. turkey should not be given additional funds to keep migrants in its country. otherwise, he'll break the terms of the agreement again and blackmail the eu. the solution is to allocate funds to ngos that are helping on the ground in refugee camps in turkey, and to prevent inequalities in the world. we keep forgetting that migration is a manifestation of inequality, whether it's about economic development, security, respect for human rights, or the threat of natural disasters and climate change. as long as these inequalities persist, we will continue to face the refugee crisis. we are preventing migrants from crossing the border in vain, because the human cost is appalling. an estimated 35,000 migrants worldwide have already lost their lives in search of a better future. let us stand in solidarity with greece and prevent a humanitarian disaster just outside the eu's borders.
in writing. for several days now, we have been receiving pictures and videos showing how the european union's services are waging war on the greek-turkish border ... with women, children, families, with people who are forced to flee from the war in their own country. where are the values of the european union? if we forget about our values, about human rights, then we forget why we are here, what our goals are, what we should stand guard over! this situation is the result of negligence by the previous union authorities. but that's history now, and the new commission, the new commission president, the new president of the european council must start acting but in line with the eu values. the community must act immediately and decisively. and it's not just about helping on the greek-turkish border, but even more about protecting the borders from refugees. it is necessary to implement a system of relocation of migrants. and as s&d president iratxe garcía pérez said, treating these people with dignity is not only a moral duty but also, and perhaps above all, a matter of respect for the law. the commission is facing three challenges: protecting the rule of law, tackling the climate crisis and tackling the migration crisis. the commission must be resolute in each of these areas, confirming that the values set out in article 2 of the treaty are not just empty words.
in writing. we're in an emergency situation that, until a few weeks ago, none of us could have imagined. this forces us to reassess our priorities. naturally, our efforts and actions must be focused on fighting the spread of this deadly virus. we must get our country back on track as soon as possible so that, once the crisis in europe has been contained, we can return to the issues we discussed at the last plenary session, such as events at the external borders of the european union, which are also in fact extremely vulnerable to the current pandemic. as the european parliament, we should give our full support to the current joint action to help combat the current threat and its consequences. the most important of these will be voted on today to speed up the ep's work on this issue as much as possible. i also hope that parliament will start work as soon as possible on a package of aid and financial support for the countries and economic operators that have been particularly affected by the current situation. we are grateful to all those who are on the front lines of the fight against the epidemic every day: health workers, police officers, military, border guards and law enforcement. we express our solidarity with all those affected by the covid-19 virus, and especially with the families of the victims.
in writing. the focus of the coronavirus pandemic has shifted to europe, and the hard part is yet to come. and we don't know how long this crisis will last. it touches us all, and it brings to light our weaknesses and vulnerabilities more clearly than ever before. turns out we're not prepared at all for a health crisis. we're unarmed, we don't have medical supplies that we can deploy immediately. we need an outside rescue. we see economies collapse, and more and more people lose their jobs. in this situation, the union must act swiftly to help the member states to adapt its action to their needs. it is good that today, with the restructuring of the structural funds, some member states are getting a breath of fresh air, but those that have previously performed well and have already committed resources are not getting a penny of that. i ask the commission to come up with a solution for them too. preparations are underway to provide financial assistance to the euro area, but please consider those outside the euro area. the commission has recently come out with a new industrial strategy and a strategy for smes, which now all need to be re-thought, taking into account the situation in each member state and complementing national measures. the survival of smes, family farms and individual entrepreneurs means the survival of european economies; let's focus on them, because they are the key to the union finding itself as soon as possible after the pandemic, at whatever cost.
in writing. the coronavirus is one of the biggest challenges facing citizens in the member states of the european union in recent decades. there is no concrete forecast for the end of the epidemic or its economic impact. however, despite the many uncertainties and contradictions, we can agree on one principle: the protection of human life is paramount. it has three main components. the first factor is health protection. we owe a debt of gratitude to the health workers who are fighting against the virus to save lives. i suggest that the european commission should give all possible support to the health systems of the member states. the preservation of jobs is also a key component of the effort to protect human life. "where there's work, there's everything" is a saying. i therefore call on the commission to continue to support member states' economic crisis management programmes, including through the mobilisation of new budgetary resources, to protect jobs after the pandemic. finally, tolerance is also an essential part of the protection of human life. so it's important that we put our differences aside now. in a situation like this, unity and common defense trumps all political ambition. as members of the european parliament, we all have to grow up to the task.
in writing. we have to act urgently because of the epidemic. in france, we can already see that the slums are the most affected by infection, because they have a higher proportion of inadequate housing conditions, and also extreme economic and social difficulties: 60% of households are below the poverty line, unemployment is 90% for the 16-25 age group, two-thirds of children are out of school, and many have underlying diseases that are conducive to viral infection. in the eastern half of europe, these figures are even worse in most cases. and statistics show that if the infection, if the epidemic, gets into these vulnerable communities, that's where it's going to do the most damage. among other things, they lack basic sanitation, clean drinking water, sewage, heating, and daily hot food. and for many of you, the coronavirus could be a life-threatening viral cocktail. in addition to the immediate intervention of health systems and economic sectors voted on today, the commission should allow member states to use unused roma integration funds to help the most disadvantaged, vulnerable and vulnerable communities. i call on the commission and the member states to take immediate, coordinated action. we can't leave anyone behind. we cannot allow those who have been vulnerable to become even more so.
in writing. the fight against the new virus pandemic is still ongoing. together, as a united and united europe, we are taking action to contain and then suppress the plague. i consider this the first, basic and good expression of cooperation. member states are closing their borders, social austerity is imposed from above, and many sectors of the economy are being curtailed. all these temporary, though radical, measures are intended to serve as a temporary method of controlling the plague. i welcome that, but we must remember that everything has its consequences. we are now on the verge of an unprecedented economic collapse, including on a global scale. it is our absolute duty to counteract this or at least to do everything in our power to weaken this specter of crisis. i am pleased that we are debating today an initiative to support member states and our citizens in these difficult times. but let us not delude ourselves, please, that these actions will suffice. we need more ambitious solutions better and more flexible means to increase public aid capacity. let us not be afraid to make firm decisions. let us prove that this institution too can fulfil its responsibilities and show common sense and credibility in the eyes of the citizens who put their hopes in us.
in writing. the coronavirus response investment initiative is the right response to the urgent need to help our smes. but fighting the recession will require much more. in addition to unprecedented amounts from national and union budgets, we must consider the concept of a fundamental modification of the green deal. whether we are for or against this idea, we must see reality as it is. two major economic challenges lie ahead for us in the coming decades: the european green deal and the coronavirus recession. taking on both of these challenges will cost a fortune and change the face of europe. but we can't afford to fund them both. there is no time for experiments and politics shaped by ideology alone. the european union has a historic opportunity to react and take the right decisions. first and foremost, we must guarantee our citizens decent health care, security and economic growth that will provide jobs and a decent standard of living. only then can we return to our political debate about how green europe should be. the covid-19 crisis has shown how fragile our economy can be. let us not take this lightly and cling to the green deal at a time when europe needs new solutions.
in writing. – in this unprecedented situation we need to be taking immediate and decisive measures to help save those who have been infected by the sars-cov-2 virus and to stop the virus from spreading. we need to be taking measures to save entrepreneurs and businesses from going bankrupt, to prevent loss of jobs and income of european citizens. at the same time we already know, that the current pandemic, even if it can be fairly quickly contained – which we all hope – has already made us aware of many facts we had not been noticing before or facts which we had been ignoring. one of these facts is that there is not enough cooperation between eu member states, that there is not enough integration and that it is too shallow. we have seen that faced with threats as grave as the threat of a pandemic, member states are likely to resort to some egoistic, nationalistic measures. but viruses, climate catastrophes do not know the notion of a nation state, they target all equally. and we can fight them only together, together we are stronger, more resilient. we need much deeper european integration.
in writing. i am pleased that, in addition to the temporary legal framework allowing member states to use the full flexibility provided for in eu rules on aid to support the economy in the context of the covid-19 epidemic, the commission, under the union civil protection mechanism (resceu), has extended the existing implementing act to allow the eu to stockpile protective equipment such as face masks and intensive care equipment and thus address shortages in response to an urgent need. what additional concrete action is the commission considering to provide practical support to italy and spain the two most affected eu countries? it would also be advisable to seek other sources of funding, such as the european globalisation adjustment fund, which has been underused in recent years. the scope of support could be modified by referring to public health emergencies. in conclusion, it is important that eu action is targeted at ensuring the supply of protective equipment throughout europe on the basis of specific guidelines. i believe that the implementing act under the 'resceu' should be extended to allow the eu to purchase all the necessary medical equipment.
in writing. even before the covid-19 pandemic, economists predicted that the global economy was heading for economic crisis. and here we are facing an unprecedented global crisis that will directly and dramatically affect us all. covid-19 has shown that we are not prepared for this kind of crisis. we see the economic and social consequences every day, but we are even more afraid of what the future will bring. underfunded and overworked health care, people out of work and on the verge of collapse, businesses and factories collapsing. we're in the middle of a recession that's going to affect every aspect of our lives. the economic crisis has become a fact and has been overshadowed by the coronavirus pandemic. it therefore welcomes the idea of solidarity and joint, coordinated action. our job at this point is to be above all about common sense and compliance. but i think this is only the first step in overcoming the crisis we are facing today. we must continue to work together in a spirit of solidarity to find new and ambitious ways of developing more flexible rules for the use of existing budgetary resources to ensure the financial liquidity of the member states.
in writing. the sars-cov-2 pandemic, also known as the coronavirus, is a challenge we have to face in our time. the situation in many countries is dramatic. there is a shortage of hospital beds, doctors and nurses, life-saving equipment and personal protective equipment, and the result is often a division between those who can survive and those who cannot. could this have been prevented? was the union's action not overdue? some member states, seeing the eu's inaction, took matters into their own hands and, through exceptional but necessary security measures, were more effective than others in containing the spread of the virus. we can and must help those who need our help. medical personnel who fight and risk their lives to save others cannot be left alone in this unequal fight. our actions cannot be pretended, we cannot resort to generalities and half-measures. member states expect rapid implementation of concrete solutions that will significantly help in the fight against the coronavirus and its effects. the effects of this are already devastating for many sectors of the european economy. we must act swiftly and decisively. we have the tools and instruments. europa, don't sleep, because the next time you wake up, it might be too late.
in writing. i bow to the medical personnel around the world who have been fighting for weeks for the lives and health of citizens in the face of the spreading coronavirus pandemic. we are facing a challenge the world has not seen in decades, an epidemic that does not tolerate neglect, mistakes and time. today, our solidarity and decisive action can save the lives and health of many more citizens, and our decisions will affect the european economy and save countries from collapse. the collapse of businesses, the unemployment, the impoverishment of society - we all feel it. in the face of such a powerful threat as covid-19, the european union has acted too late and too slowly, putting the solidarity of nations to the greatest test since the second world war. we urgently need a programme to rebuild europe in line with the marshall plan. we need a comprehensive package of measures and a determination in the decisions of the commission and the ep to fight effectively against the crisis on two fronts: health security and the economy. flexible approaches to shifting resources or creating green corridors are just the beginning of a common struggle. the challenge is clear: to reassess the objectives we have set for europe in the years ahead. the pandemic that will pass is a test for the people of a united europe and a test of european cooperation and responsibility and an answer to the question of whether we have done our best to respond effectively and in time to the tragedies of entrepreneurs, workers and families in every country of a united europe.
in writing. the coronavirus pandemic has exposed the weaknesses of the member states, but also of the community as a whole. in each area of member states' activity, there are areas where the eu can and should play a more prominent role. the crisis has shown that it is time to start debating new areas of union competence, such as the common health policy. the area that requires full eu coordination is the control of the epidemic, the treatment of the sick and the prevention of infections. the eu cannot be just a funder in such situations, but must be an efficient management organisation, taking consistent decisions across the community. every european woman and every european man should have equal access to medical care, especially in situations of imminent danger to health and life. it is also a question of security in the context of the free movement of persons within the community. the european union should also be able to provide the necessary financial support to the countries of the region, in particular through the european regional development fund. the eu is not just a single organism socially and politically, but also economically. the policy on the use of restrictions on freedom of economic activity in crisis situations therefore requires harmonisation. the eu should maximise its support and protection activities in this area, including for example insurance to enable commercial insurers to pay compensation to businesses.
in writing. the coronavirus pandemic is a huge challenge for the eu as a whole. this is a test first and foremost for our health care systems, for our economies, and for our society as a whole. the negative impact of the pandemic on european economies is still difficult to assess, but we can already see that its effects will be felt for many years to come. effective action to combat the pandemic requires immediate action and the swift mobilisation of all available eu funds. i support the commission's proposal for a 37 billion euro investment initiative in response to the coronavirus pandemic. i very much hope that it will mitigate the impact of the epidemic by triggering investment in health systems and other sectors of the economy. my reservation is that the scope of the changes proposed by the commission is, in my view, insufficient in the face of the scale of the challenges. i call on the commission to make further efforts to make the rules more flexible and to prepare another, more comprehensive package of changes to support member states in their fight against covid-19. in these difficult times and in these extraordinary circumstances, let us be united and responsible. i believe that with courage and determination in action, consistency and common concern, we will overcome this crisis. but for that to happen, we must take effective and decisive action, even at the cost of some inconvenience and personal limitations. i believe we can do this together.

decide which supplies we have to have simply here at home. therefore, we are opening special storage facilities where we are stockpiling the most important medical equipment and medicines. but we also here in europe, just to be sure that when we would need it most, we will simply have it. therefore, i think that all of you who said that we need a more ambitious, more strategic, and more united procurement, which would make sure that our doctors, our nurses and our citizens have all they need for their work. i also would like to applaud european industries, where more and more companies are converting their usual production to produce masks, disinfectant gels, or simply started the production of ventilators, which are so much in need in our hospitals. i believe that in a couple of months, with the strong power of the european industry, we will show what i believe will be very impressive results. ms ries raised the issue of the elderly and the most vulnerable. my mother and my mother-in-law in slovakia are in a similar situation. therefore, we adapted the funds for european aid for the most deprived and most vulnerable. let’s have a look together and see if the adaptation is far-reaching enough – what can we do more to make sure that we would help also those who need it most? to conclude, i would just quickly react to two very important remarks. one by mr caspary, who was raising the issue of the virus-tracing app. here i would like to reassure all of you that what we are talking about will be a european app on which the best expertise that europe can offer is used; that it will be tracing the virus and not tracking people; that it will fully respect protection of personal data. it would be voluntary for the people who would like to use it. it will be anonymous, and in practice it should work in a way that it would inform you by text message that you might have been exposed to the virus and you should take the necessary precautions. mr verhofstadt, multiannual financial perspective. but we also know that to get there, a lot of diplomacy is required, because the decision on mff is unanimous, and therefore we are working extensively, especially our president, talking to the leaders, making sure that the proposal we put on the table would be ambitious enough but at the same time will be supported by all eu member states, because this is what we need at this point in time. we want to learn from the past. we want to use leverage. we want to use the best of our policies, which deliver good services and progress to our member states. and i believe that all these would be properly reflected in our next proposals. to conclude, i just really would like to thank all of you for your ideas, for your suggestions and the support you demonstrated today, during all these very difficult weeks, and i believe that with your support we will build the new europe, which will emerge from this dramatic crisis.

in writing. can we blame hungary for being one of the first countries in europe to take decisive steps in the fight against the coronavirus? as early as 10 april, the hungarian government began to introduce regulations aimed at limiting the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on the national economy and labor market. for example, special economic zones, where investments of national economic importance are located, have been excluded from the management of local governments and placed under the administration of the state, with the tax paid being taken over. these decisions preceded the introduction on 30 march of decrees suspending certain legal acts, prohibiting the holding of by-elections and referendums, increasing the penalties for breaking the quarantine order or spreading false information about the pandemic. the hungarian government's actions have allowed production to resume in april by the largest manufacturing plants, including audi, mercedes, opel and suzuki. thanks to the government's quick and decisive action, not only has the economy's losses been reduced and the blackout stopped, but the number of infected people in hungary remains lower than in the czech republic or austria (five times lower). these figures show the correctness of the decisions taken by the government of viktor orbán, which is effectively protecting its country and its citizens from the raging pandemic.
in writing. as a hungarian representative and a hungarian patriot, i am extremely sad that once again the policy of the hungarian government is on the agenda. hungary deserves better than this. let's face it, this is real. the mzp launched the 'dictatorship monitor' application on its online platform, which tracks the excesses that fidesz is carrying out under the guise of protecting against the coronavirus. there are countless of them. in recent days, for example, the spread of fear has led to more arrests by the police for criticizing the government's handling of the epidemic on social media. fidesz's immorality is also evidenced by the way it uses the epidemic to take out opposition mayors: in recent days, a proposal was submitted referring to the emergency that takes tax revenues and driving licenses from the (opposition) municipalities selected by the government and gives them to the fidesz-led county municipalities. it is utterly shameful that the hungarian government is using even this epidemic situation for political revenge and booty-grabbing. now that we are deciding on the next seven-year budget, the question must be how to sanction an anti-eu government in a member state without any damage to the country or its citizens. i propose that we pay the eu funds to join the european public prosecutor's office. until orbán is willing to do so, he cannot decide on the distribution of european resources! the proposals will be judged by independent decision-makers in brussels. it cannot continue to feed its oligarchs and its stealth dictatorship with eu funds.
in writing. the coronavirus pandemic puts all european societies in a situation where the risks of breach of the rule of law and democratic principles are higher than usual. societies that have already been swept under the rug by these principles are in danger of being dragged deeper and deeper into a cycle of authoritarianism. once you're in a spiral like this, once you're in it deep enough, it's very difficult to get back up. hungary is now very close to this frontier and its democracy is close to collapse. as regards hungary, my concern is not just with the exceptional legislation but with the longer-term development of the country. in hungary, the orbán government has systematically restricted the freedom of movement of the media, civil society and science, and has concentrated power in a way that is not in line with the rules of a democratic society. the situation in hungary has been brought to europe far too late. the hungarian authorities have not provided any evidence that the hungarian authorities have taken the necessary measures to ensure that the rule of law is respected in the country. it's not taken seriously until the damage has already been done. it is clear that at the latest now all the measures that have been considered too onerous in the past must be fully implemented. the article 7 procedure must be accelerated and hungary must be put in a situation where its voting rights in the council are threatened. more importantly, the eu's financial resources will be cut off. they are the life thread of viktor orbán, with which he builds his own centrally controlled capitalism, where the winners are the powerful and their inner circle.
in writing. it is really incomprehensible why during the pandemic we are dealing with the rule of law in hungary, and specifically with the alleged violation of it by the extraordinary measures introduced, as in many other member states, to effectively fight the pandemic. moreover, the form in which this debate is conducted does not allow the hungarian government to present arguments in its defence. this is contrary to the principle of due process, which is also a fundamental principle of the rule of law. if the president of the ep had allowed the representative of the hungarian government to speak, we would have learned that the state of emergency law does not give the government unlimited powers. they will end with the end of the pandemic, or even earlier, if parliament so decides. the european commission is aware of this and therefore does not initiate infringement proceedings against a member state. today's debate is further proof of the double standards in the eu.

from this crisis together.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, 75 years ago, the guns of the second world war in europe fell silent. the nazi regime was defeated, but europe lay in ruins. just five years later, on 9 may 1950, robert schuman made a declaration that would profoundly change this continent and would put it on a path that no one could have anticipated. for me, this is a very special moment. seventy years ago, robert schuman started a journey, step by step. he showed us the way and the direction. and today, here we are. just seven days ago, at the eu—western balkans summit, we laid the ground for reuniting the western balkans with our union, reuniting europe’s history with its geography. yes, today, our union faces its greatest challenge yet: a pandemic that knows no borders, a pandemic that threatens our lives and our way of life, a pandemic that has tested our union to its core. but, as so often in history, this crisis has also shown europe’s greatest strengths: our commitment to unity, born of common values and shared history, and our solidarity with those in need. schuman’s words resonate today more strongly than ever before: ‘it is no longer a time for vain words, but for a bold, constructive act’. the schuman declaration embodied the perfect balance, the delicate dance between idealism and pragmatism, without which there would be no european union and no european solidarity as we know it today. he famously said, ‘europe will not be made all at once according to a single plan. it will be built through concrete achievements which first create a de facto solidarity.’ this crisis has put that solidarity to the hardest of tests. in march, some even said that we would not pass these tests. but, if you look around the world today, europe has become the beating heart of solidarity: french patients treated in german hospitals, polish doctors and romanian nurses working in italy, and a huge recovery plan is in the making. the world is watching. our european model will only mean something to the world if we show solidarity within our union’s borders, to each other, and beyond, with our partners globally. since the pandemic began, the european union has been working on all fronts to contain the spread of the coronavirus, support health systems, protect and save lives, and counter the socioeconomic impacts of the pandemic, with historically unprecedented measures at both national and eu level. the commission will directly support the healthcare systems of eu countries with eur 3 billion from the eu budget, matched with eur 3 billion from the member states to fund the emergency support instrument and the resceu common stockpile of equipment. the resceu initiative helps secure vital equipment, from ventilators to personal protective equipment, and to mobilise medical teams for assistance to the most vulnerable, including in refugee camps. the first hosting state of this stockpile is romania. the production of the first ventilators has started, and some 330 000 protective masks were delivered to spain, italy and croatia in the past weeks. since the beginning of the outbreak, thanks to the eu civil protection mechanism and consular protection coordination, the european union has brought home over half a million citizens stranded all over the world. thanks to the emergency support instrument, the european union has procured another 10 million masks, the first 1.5 million of which have already been delivered to 17 member states. i want to thank this house for having launched the ‘europeans against covid—19’ campaign. this europe day, the commission and the council joined forces with you, and we all pay tribute to those who are making history today, the everyday heroes fighting the coronavirus in our hospitals, in research labs, or by delivering personal protective equipment to those in need, because we know that coronavirus knows no borders. tackling this pandemic is a global challenge and the eu is leading the global effort to develop and deploy effective diagnostics, treatments and a vaccine. without this tool, every country in the world remains vulnerable. countries and international organisations are joining forces to develop these tools and put the structures in place that ensure they are universally available and affordable. how wealthy a country is should not determine whether its people get to live without this virus. that is why president von der leyen launched an international pledging marathon on 4 may. so far, we have raised eur 7.4 billion, and this includes a pledge of eur 1.4 billion from the commission. but we know that more is needed and i am confident it will come. the crisis gives us an opportunity to lead by example and to reach for our highest aspirations, even when, in the short term, it might be easier to give in to our lowest instincts. we will be remembered tomorrow for how we act today. therefore, this crisis forces us to reflect. the pandemic will have a lasting effect, not just on the global system, but also on our daily lives. it is vital that on our path to recovery, we reach out, engage and listen to citizens, at european, national, regional and local level. the conference on the future of europe is an ideal forum for that and should commence as soon as conditions allow it. the conference, as a pan—european democratic exercise, can reinforce the link between european citizens and the institutions. it can help rebuild trust and solidarity, even in the new coronavirus reality. the context might have changed, but our determination has not. we want the conference on the future of europe to give citizens a greater say in shaping future eu policies, and we want this to be a joint exercise, involving the european parliament, the council and the commission on an equal footing. that is also why any decision on when to launch the conference must be a joint one taken by all three institutions. given the circumstances, my colleague and friend, vice—president šuica, who is leading the commission’s efforts on the conference, is following this debate remotely from croatia. she is very much looking forward to joining the debates in this house in a physical mode as soon as possible. in order to be ready for the launch of the conference under the containment measures scenario, the commission is exploring digital solutions to enable us to host virtual debates and dialogues. we are working on a multilingual digital platform, allowing citizens to share their results and promote interactive ways for public engagement as part of the conference. such a digital platform would be open to all eu institutions. but a digital solution alone cannot reach everyone and cannot compensate for the real deal: face—to—face town hall discussions and workshops across the continent, reaching people from all walks of life. to protect the health of our citizens, we need to be patient and plan accordingly, step by step. once the council has adopted its mandate, we will get there. i am confident that the next step, the joint declaration by the parliament, the commission and the council, which is necessary to launch the conference, is within reach. a little more than 30 years ago, i was looking through the barbed wire of the infamous iron curtain to austria. this fence was just two kilometres from our apartment and i passed it every single day. i could see the people, the houses and the lights on the other side of the danube, but i was told by my father that i would never be able to cross the border. therefore, for me, the schuman declaration celebration is also a celebration of the european dream and freedom. i am sure that robert schuman would be proud today of how much we have accomplished. but i am also convinced that he would push us higher and further. therefore, let’s respond to his inspiration by building an even fairer, greener, freer and stronger europe. in writing. the 70th anniversary of the schuman declaration, the first step in the construction of europe, comes at a most difficult time for europe since the end of the second world war, but one in which the full significance of the declaration and the ideal of 'ever closer union' which it embodies are even more apparent. the unprecedented health, economic and social crisis that the covid-19 pandemic has generated demonstrates how timely the awareness contained in the declaration is that europe must emerge "from concrete achievements that first create de facto solidarity", and that only "an organised and vital europe" can truly contribute, in addition to "civilization" and "maintaining peaceful relations", to the protection of its citizens and the promotion of the values of freedom, equality, justice, legality, protection of fundamental rights and respect for the rule of law. the need for solidarity, coordination and joint action, underlying the declaration, has never been more evident: in particular, in the immediate as well as in the medium and long term, european solidarity is and will be essential if no one is to be left behind. it is therefore essential to strengthen european institutions and policies, their effectiveness and their democratic character: only by persevering in the spirit of the declaration will the union be able to meet the difficult challenges of the present historic moment.

in writing. the schuman declaration is the cornerstone of the european communities and the union today. on the occasion of the 70th anniversary of its signature, it is worth recalling that the declaration, also known as the schuman plan, was not only about the coordination of coal and steel production in the ecsc countries, but above all about the idea of creating a european federation based on common values derived from greek philosophy, roman law and christian humanism. this overarching objective of the schuman declaration was transposed in 1957 into the treaty of rome and is still codified there as a process of creating an ever closer union between the peoples of europe. we are at a very special moment of integration. on the one hand, we are celebrating the 70th anniversary of the signing of the schuman declaration and the 10th anniversary of the treaty of lisbon, and on the other, we are experiencing an unprecedented pandemic crisis with multi-dimensional health, economic and institutional implications. the european union and its member states should seize this moment to step up and emerge from this crisis stronger. not only by building on the pro-integration mechanisms of the lisbon treaty (bridge clauses), but also by developing more far-reaching proposals, such as strengthening the european parliament's position, introducing a general principle of qualified majority voting in the council and constitutionalising the european pillar of social rights. the conference on the future of europe will certainly be a great opportunity to do so.

in writing. today's discussion on the use of smartphone apps in managing the spread of a pandemic is crucial not only in the context of the gradual lifting of restrictions on freedom of movement in the union, but also in the context of protecting the privacy of eu citizens. mobile applications are being developed and are already used in some member states to track people infected or at risk of infection. such applications can play an important and positive role in the process of easing pandemic restrictions and gradually returning to normal. however, they also have a disproportionate impact on our fundamental rights, such as data protection and privacy. while the protection of human life and public health is of paramount importance to all of us, both at eu and national level, it must be strongly emphasised that governments and the private sector cannot promote the use of untested technologies with the potential to infringe our rights. the long history of emergency measures in crisis situations shows that often when surveillance is introduced, it goes too far, fails to achieve its objectives and, on many occasions, despite the resolution of a crisis, its operation is prolonged without justification. mobile surveillance programmes, which can undoubtedly be temporary measures to contain the pandemic until the expected vaccine is available, cannot under any circumstances become a permanent part of the extended surveillance system.
in writing. – the european union and the eu member states must find coordinated common approach to support the gradual lifting of confinement measures. the group of socialists and democrats in the european parliament (s&d) supports joint approaches, but also underlines the importance of privacy and data protection aspects of every possible digital solutions. i believe that every contact tracing app must comply with eu data protection and privacy rules and should be based on anonymised data. they can complement existing manual contact tracing and according to some member states these applications can help interrupt the transmission chain of the virus, but the use of them must strictly remain voluntary-based and cannot be linked as condition to other rights, such as border crossings, employment or to entering to public institutions.
in writing. – digital solutions such as contact tracing applications are essential in the fight against covid-19, particularly as countries ease lockdown measures. however, strong privacy safeguards must be essential. thus far the commission has maintained that contact tracing apps should guarantee privacy, should not store unnecessary personal information including location tracking, should be installed voluntarily, and dismantled post-pandemic. although these safeguards are essential, they must also be enforced on a member state level and there must be interoperability between different contact tracing applications. additionally, the commission must enforce independent app reviews and audits on a member state level. these apps must be frequently checked for privacy, transparency, and functional usability concerns, especially as the covid-19 is still evolving. the commission should help the member states assemble a team of cross-sector experts for these reviews. medical experts should determine that these apps can be effectively integrated into different phases of virus containment. technical and data experts should consistently guarantee privacy and functionality. legal experts must continuously develop and provide regulatory framework and legislation updates on data collection and data destruction. further, this entire process must be extremely transparent so that the public feels comfortable using the apps.
in writing. the right to privacy is a fundamental human right. it is guaranteed by international legal acts, european law and the polish constitution article 47 of the basic law speaks directly about it. the right to privacy is not an absolute right, however, as even in the most democratic countries it can be limited by important public interests. however, such restrictions must be imposed on the basis of generally applicable law and must be necessary and proportionate. this is very important because any invasion of an individual's privacy is an invasion of their freedom. the coronavirus pandemic has left governments in many countries facing a dilemma of whether to control the movement of citizens in the name of controlling the spread of the pandemic or not to risk interfering with their freedom. because we know that such interference is always an opportunity for abuse. especially since current technologies allow for surveillance on a large scale. most eu governments have chosen the first option: in poland, for example, the home quarantine app is used. i'm not opposed to solutions that are designed to monitor the movement of pandemics. after all, it is about protecting the health and lives of the people of the union. however, i would like to emphasize that such measures must be proportionate and serve monitoring rather than surveillance. they must also be consistent at eu level: the protection of the right to privacy should not be less for some and more for others.
in writing. new digital technologies and services bring not only benefits but also risks. the benefits when they serve citizens, the risks when they are used to mass surveillance of citizens, invasion of privacy and violation of basic human rights under the guise of protecting citizens in times of crisis. there is evidence that crises are used to introduce surveillance tools that are maintained after the crisis and used for other purposes, such as not only controlling distance between people, but also crowd control and citizen surveillance. this could lead to the creation of totalitarian states. furthermore, databases can become a target for hackers. our privacy and freedom on the one hand, and our security on the other, are not mutually exclusive, but on the contrary, we can only feel safe when our privacy and freedom are upheld, and not living in a state that can unlimitedly interfere with our privacy. the state's power to monitor the entire population is dangerous for democracy, freedom and civil rights. there is a presumption of innocence. therefore, the prosecution and the courts must consider each case individually. the way to ensure real security is to effectively prosecute individual cases of breach of the law and to punish the perpetrators consistently. if we fail to be aware of these threats, new technologies and digital services could lead to the end of human freedom.
in writing. effective fight against covid-19 on all fronts is paramount to ensure we return to normalcy and prevent further economic collapse. the contact tracing application in the fight against coronavirus should provide security for the health and information of eu citizens. maximum security for sensitive data, decentralisation, interoperability of systems, specific application times, cooperation of all member states in developing the solution are all elements that make us all trust the new technologies. consultation with the medical community and ngos, industry and business organisations, as well as full voluntary use, are of the utmost importance. a great example of rapid response, good cooperation and world-class security is the protego safe application implemented by poland. this is a fully decentralised solution unrelated to, for example, the 'home quarantine' application, intended for a different user group and serving different purposes. it is tested for cybersecurity on an ongoing basis, does not use location data, does not require the provision of your name, pesel number, telephone number or other identifying data, unlike solutions in some eu countries, and will only be used to prevent covid-19 infection. let us use the good practices of member states to minimise the interference with the privacy of eu citizens. we want all eu citizens to have such gdpr-compliant solutions so that they feel safe, are happy to use innovative solutions and protect themselves by protecting others.

mr president, we are facing a decisive moment: either we are ambitious or we will not survive. this 750 billion euro plan presented by the commission is ambitious, and therefore also represents hope. however, much work remains to be done. first, parliament must be involved in the design of the recovery plan. europe needs, in addition to this economic marshall plan, a democratic marshall plan which defends the rule of law and our values as strongly as we defend our single currency. secondly, we need guarantees that this fund will be distributed fairly and equitably and that it will reach the citizens; that the billions of euros we are announcing today will be real. citizens no longer believe us when we say the word "billions". too many times it's meant nothing to them. thirdly, it is urgent that this fund should be made available as soon as possible. millions and millions of people in europe cannot wait. the ruin kills more than the virus. fourthly, this plan cannot be implemented at the expense of reducing the european budget. we don't have different needs, we just have more needs now. fifthly, the fund cannot be used to whitewash the policies of bad governments. if we water populism, it's a plant that will grow and take root. sixth, we are 27 states that put the money in and 27 states that collect the money. let us not be fooled: money does not fall from the sky, sooner or later citizens will have to put it in. so this plan must think of the citizens and not the governments. it's time for the welfare state to show its muscle. seventhly, the financial framework cannot compromise the next financial framework. the national parliaments will ultimately have to approve this plan. conclusion: the economy is not about numbers, the economy is about trust. we are talking about human beings. we are talking about the lives of all our fellow citizens, not the politicians who rule them.
mr. president, we are facing a historic day today. because it can certainly be the beginning of a fundamental and irrevocable change in the process of building the european union. a change similar, by the way, to that which the introduction of the euro meant. the joint issuance of debt represents a fundamental change in the economic and social fabric of our union. it is a step we have been working towards for decades and today we have a proposal from this commission which is aimed in that direction. i think that this communication, this review, this design of the recovery fund is a reasonable proposal, it is a sound proposal, it needs to be analysed, because obviously we have not had time to know the details, but i would like to take this opportunity to ask the council and to ask the members of this parliament to make a final effort, an additional effort to take this historic step for the benefit of all europeans.
madam president, this is a very important package. it is a very significant leap forward in the integration of the euro area, and it is a political message to our citizens: we are going to go into debt together to face the crisis together. obviously, we wanted more, we wanted a bigger package, one that had a bigger macroeconomic impact. i would venture to say that this is probably the minimum to save our euro area and our internal market. and a very clear message to the council: the future of thousands of european citizens cannot be held hostage to what four governments - and i say four governments, not four countries - want, which are not up to date. on the question of conditionality, which is going to be the subject of a very important debate, i want to say three things which i think are very relevant. the first one, yes to the digital transition, of course; yes to the ecological transition. let us not forget the social component in societies that are still very much affected by the previous crisis. second, we democratize the system of designing reforms. it is not possible for technocratic recommendations to reach the states without parliamentary control. and thirdly, above all, let us not go back too quickly to the anti-social reforms and austerity which have done so much damage to our societies in the past. let us make this a useful instrument for the future of our citizens.

vice-president of the commission. – thank you very much madam president, honourable members of the european parliament, my dear colleagues from the european commission. first, i really would like to thank you for what i felt was very strong, overwhelming support in most of the interventions for the ambitious proposal the commission has tabled today. and i really would like to thank you for the inspiration, which on many occasions we have drawn from this house, from your resolutions, from the debates that we had with you, when we’ve been looking for ways to best respond to your calls for demonstrating more solidarity, for using this crisis as an opportunity to modernise the european economy and for consolidating the position of europe as a global actor and global player. we put forward proposals, which was never done before. it’s really without precedent, because what we wanted to do was to adapt the initial multiannual financial perspective proposal to the current needs and because we fully realised that the economic crisis is so sharp and so deep, we knew that we need to come up with a new instrument, which we named next generation eu. altogether, we are talking about eur 1.1 trillion of the proposal for mff, an additional eur 750 billion for the next generation instrument, which would be divided between grants and loans, as you suggested in your resolution. i very much appreciate that mr weber, ms garcía pérez and mr cioloș supported this approach and i would like to reassure you that we know that the success of the results – if we invest the money in the right areas, and we definitely want to do that – we fully realise that if we want to modernise the european economy, we have to invest in green, sustainable technologies. we have to be much more digital than we are right now, and we have to learn our lessons for improving the resilience of the european economy, because we learned how difficult it is to be dependent on some global value chains or single supplier of such sensitive health materials as we have seen over the last few months. so what we have put on the table is that the proposal has to not only overcome the crisis, but has to modernise, has to respect the important social aspects of our policy and has to make europe really ready for the post-covid 21st-century world. a lot of questions – and some of them presented with a great vigour – have been linked to debts and also to own resources – mr meuthen, ms aubry, mr van overtveldt. here again, i would like to tell you that we did our homework. we studied the issue very carefully and we have come up with different options for own resources, which you want to, of course, explore with you and with the member states. we want to use the new ets revenues, which will be coming eventually from the aviation and maritime sector, to use them for financing parts of the mff in the future. we are considering the so-called ‘single market tax’, especially from those companies which are benefiting from the fact that the single market is so big and functions that well. we will be following carefully how other countries and powers on this planet are respecting the paris goals and if they are really reducing the carbon footprint of their products and their economy, and we will be ready to proceed if necessary with a carbon adjustment tax which, again, could be revenue for the european budget. and we are, of course, not forgetting about the possibility of digital taxation where, of course, we want to have a global agreement, preferably within the oecd or g20, but if this did not work, we are ready to consider to go alone. and ms szydło and mr azmani have highlighted the importance of tax evasion and unfair tax practices. this is, of course, one of the priorities upon which we are going to focus, and for us, the proper execution of the european budget and proper tax collection is, of course, one of the key priorities. to be quite honest, i didn’t quite get the comment of the honourable member, mr gyöngyösi, who was criticising us for lack of transparency. at 12 o’clock, we in the college adopted these very important proposals, and at one o’clock the whole college was here. the european parliament was the first audience where we presented our proposals, where our president went into great detail about what we want to do and how we want to accomplish it. and therefore, i think that that tradition where we fully respect the democratic scrutiny of the european parliament would be, of course, maintained in the future, and we will be debating with you all of the legislative proposals, which are very complex and where we need close cooperation and very close consultation. there’ve been several questions linked with state aid. i have to say that my colleague, executive vice-president vestager, is known for her vigour in reviewing and assessing every single application, and we also have to agree that these last three months have been totally exceptional. at first, we had to fight for the lives of our citizens, then for the livelihoods and for jobs, and this is what we’ve been, with your help, doing since the beginning of this year. if you allow me, madam president, to conclude with a plea, with a request. because i think that we are at a truly historic european moment where we need – all of us – to show clear political leadership. we would very much appreciate the strong support of the european parliament, as mr gonzález pons has highlighted. but we also need your help to convince your compatriots back home. therefore, i’m also addressing this request towards the council and towards the member states, because we need a good decision. we need a quick decision, and of course we need to work very closely with all national parliaments as well, because in the end, when we are talking about the head-rooms, ceilings and own resources, we need also the positive ratification of the national parliaments. therefore, what we need is true political leadership, which would help europe to overcome the crisis and really to prepare it for the next phase. so my last sentence would be directed to all of us: let’s do this effort for the european union. let’s do it for the next generation, and let’s do it to demonstrate to our citizens that we know how to overcome the crisis and how we can prepare europe for the 21st century. president-in-office of the council. – madam president, first, i would like to thank the house for this debate and i will convey its views to my colleagues and to the president of the european council and his team. as i said in my opening intervention, the council has started preparatory work on the commission proposals so as to create the conditions for the agreement as soon as possible. as i already mentioned, yesterday, in a video conference, the eu affairs ministers, have discussed the principles and the elements that needed to be addressed in shaping the instruments that will help to kick-start the european economy and achieve its medium and long-term priorities, such as cohesion, convergence, solidarity, flexibility and inclusiveness, as well as restoring a functioning single market and strengthening the resilience and strategic autonomy of the eu in face of future challenges. they stressed the need to make the funds available immediately and in a sufficient amount. offsetting the immediate negative impact of the crisis is important for the eu’s credibility. these discussions will continue in the coming days and weeks at all council levels. we are hopeful that the member states’ positions would be converging in order to have a timely agreement on the next eu budget, which will also be discussed by the european council. the council will need guidance from the european council before it can form its position. the european parliament shares our sense of urgency on the mff, whose speedy adoption has far-reaching consequences for our citizens, our businesses and our local and regional authorities, as mentioned here. the presidency will continue to listen carefully to parliament’s position and look forward to the continued cooperation between our two institutions to prepare the ground for an ambitious, forward-looking mff and to provide a strong response to our current and future challenges.
in writing. – health policy is national competence and the eu only supports national crisis management, but we have to admit member states’ governments and the european union itself missed the opportunity to coordinate the national public health responses in the initial stage of the covid-19 outbreak. the effect of these uncoordinated national responses undermined the core european value and principles. fortunately, the union and member states still have the chance to change their attitude when realizing their exit strategies. the effective operation of the single market depends on how we exit from this crisis. the asymmetric covid-19 policies have already created conflicting interests. the suspension of the free movement of persons undermines citizens’ sense of belonging to the eu. moreover, the dissonance of the national regulations also undermine our common european values, such as well functioning cross-border co-operations and unnecessarily reduces interstate labour mobility. such rules put in very difficult situation businesses offering cross-border services, also based on them production might be halted or reduced because of disrupt supply changes. this can be even more harmful for smaller member states such as luxembourg which is more affected by closing borders in the single market. therefore, member states’ reactions must be better coordinated.
in writing. confidence in european institutions for major crises is not always fully shared by our fellow citizens. on the other hand, it is always expected of these citizens that these same institutions will take the initiative to get out of the crisis. the union faces major challenges in the years ahead, even greater than the financial crisis of 2008. in this case, we have the opportunity for the two trillion euro recovery plan to be a balance between solidarity and discipline for our multiannual financial framework. similarly, this aid must in no way be detrimental to the annual accounts of the member states; everything must be financed from the union's own resources, a concept 'of own resources' which will undoubtedly become more important as the crisis unfolds. in a world where nationalism, empty speeches and the lack of longterm plans are prevailing, europe can once again be that beacon of wisdom and longterm reference for the rest of the countries, as it has always been.
in writing. from a french point of view, the recovery plan is a real scam, since france is once again a net contributor as it has been for a long time to the european budget. this is a reminder of the weakness of the european union, which is built around a limited number of states able to make a financial contribution. this imbalance will only become more pronounced with the departure of the united kingdom and the planned enlargement to the western balkans. there is no doubt that the forthcoming negotiations between member states will be perilous. it is also unacceptable that the european union should take advantage of a crisis situation to arrogate new prerogatives and new resources to itself in defiance of the fierce opposition of public opinion in some member states. the digital tax is a sea serpent that has been revived in mrs von der leyen's words. it is therefore illusory to see in this recovery plan a new impetus for the european union, since it will only sharpen the existing divisions between the north, the east and the south. there can be no union between such disparate states, and the next wave of enlargement will soon have underlined this fact once again.
in writing. today's extraordinary plenary session of the european parliament was convened to launch a discussion with the commission and the european council on a corrective package for the eu. millions of europeans are waiting for real help in this emergency. they are not waiting for declarations, but for the tools they can use to save their work, often for their entire lives. the reality around us is that nothing is given to us once and for all, and the sense of security we have today is far from what we had at the beginning of this year. we need to work together to get back to as close as we can to where we were before the current pandemic, and that's a huge challenge in itself. but that is what the citizens of europe expect. economic security is of the utmost importance. we cannot allow an economic collapse both in our countries and in the eu as a whole. the union budget's priorities will certainly need to be reviewed, especially in order to be prepared for similar situations in the near future. we hope that mrs von der leyen's declarations today will be realistic, calling for the rejection of prejudice and stereotypes. unfortunately, my country has experienced this kind of discrimination many times before and it still does, right here in this building and in this institution. i hope that the challenges we face together today will help change that.
in writing. in its resolutions of 17 april and 15 may 2020, the european parliament called on the commission to present a massive package of measures and investments for recovery and reconstruction, in support of the european economy. the unprecedented economic and social crisis triggered by the covid-19 pandemic is europe's most difficult moment in the last 70 years and therefore requires immediate responses that are relevant to the challenges we face. the commission is today proposing the 'next generation eu', a new recovery instrument of 750 billion, which will be added to the 1100 billion of the new mff and the other instruments, for a recovery commitment of 2400 billion in total. it is an ambitious plan, which reflects the awareness that no member state can tackle this serious crisis alone and the need for genuine european solidarity, and which also recognises the role of parliament in tackling the emergency. the negotiations on the proposal must now take place under the urgency recognised by the croatian presidency, so that it can immediately address the needs and requirements of citizens, workers and businesses, ensure social cohesion and foster rapid and sustainable recovery and development.
in writing. europe is facing one of the worst crises since its inception and a decisive response is key to a rapid recovery. i welcome the commission's proposal to provide an additional €750 billion to deal with the crisis. the money will be used primarily to strengthen existing eu programmes. i am particularly pleased that the compromise proposal is also good for slovenia, which will receive more than eur 5 billion from the funds. i also welcome the historic decision to finance the debt by allowing the eu to borrow on its own in the financial markets, including through bonds, and to finance the debt with new own resources such as carbon and digital taxes. but i'm afraid the new own resources won't be enough. the socialists and democrats have also been advocating for many years the introduction of a european tax on financial transactions, a uniform taxation of capital, especially multinational capital, and the final abolition of tax havens and highly tax-friendly regimes for capital, which would bring additional resources to both the european and national budgets. the commitments to a fair europe for people, not for capital, that we have been advocating for many years in the sd, have become more urgent than ever with this crisis. but we must not allow the burden of additional debt to fall on people or future generations.
in writing. the presentation of "next generation eu", a €750 billion plan, of which €500 billion is a lost-and-found, is not only an important signal to counter the coronavirus emergency, it is also a historic achievement for europe and italy, which should be allocated the largest share of the resources. the european commission's response is the development of the proposal put forward by italy at the time, on the initiative of the president of the council, giuseppe conte, who from the outset asked europe for an ambitious plan, capable of responding effectively to the serious crisis caused by the exceptional and exceptional historical moment we are living through. a plan whereby aid to the countries and sectors most affected by the pandemic would be translated into the best and least selfish of solutions. it contains concrete proposals and objectives historically dear to the five star movement: green new deal, energy transition, and digitization. the european council now has the final say. the health, social and economic crisis caused by the coronavirus is reducing the time needed for negotiations, and i hope that the council will be able to see solidarity and unity of purpose on the part of those countries which are still calling for measures and solutions that are only in the direction of borrowing.
in writing. from a hungarian point of view, it is a success that the new recovery facility is not proposed to be set up at the expense of regional development programmes and the common agricultural policy. however, the previous criticisms of the mff by two thirds of member states, including hungary, were also justified in the light of the new proposal, which was almost unchanged from the previous proposals. hungary has achieved remarkable economic success in recent years and is also at the forefront of the management of the epidemic. it would be unjustified not to benefit from the recovery resources because we have managed the epidemic successfully and have reduced our public debt over the years through a disciplined fiscal policy. as in the case of cohesion policy, it is important for the recovery facility that the allocation of resources also takes into account differences in economic development between member states and the state of the economic sectors affected by the crisis. we cannot have poorer member states financing richer ones. the €750 billion in the recovery facility will be raised by the european commission through the use of long-term loans. the loan will be repaid by the member states over 30 years in proportion to their contributions to the eu's general budget. hungary has to repay eur 7.5 billion of the 750 billion debt at a rate of 1%. in the face of this debt, it is unacceptable that our country should receive a non-repayable aid of only €8.1 billion, which is barely more than the amount of this debt.
in writing. an ambitious common budget and a recovery facility are needed to overcome the pandemic crisis and boost our economies. it is important that the rules of the game can only be changed by consensus; that the introduction of new conditions can only be decided by complete agreement. the recovery facility should be made available from surplus resources and should not undermine traditional policies such as cohesion or agricultural policy. cohesion policy is a key element for the proper functioning of the internal market; without reducing disparities in development, there is no competitiveness and it is therefore important that its funding is not reduced. hungary is at the forefront of the management of the epidemic and its effects. as a result, the impact of the coronavirus crisis on the hungarian economy is expected to be less severe than the eu average. however, it would be unjustified to exclude the central and eastern european member states from the adequate allocation of funds because they have managed the epidemic successfully and have reduced their public debt over the years through a disciplined fiscal policy. the crisis has affected all countries; it is important that they benefit from the recovery facility in a fair manner and on the same terms, whether they are member states within or outside the euro area. the poorest member states must not finance the richest. as regards the objectives of the recovery facility, the development of the missing transport and energy infrastructure, in particular in the central and eastern european regions, should be considered a priority alongside the transition to a green economy and digitalisation.
