in writing. the european union is a community based on the equality of all states. poland does not agree to be a second-tier country where other states interfere in its internal politics, which is outside the eu's competence. the current eu pressure is a political act and has nothing to do with the rule of law. we have our rights, poland has the right to reform, it was the poles in democratic elections who decided that changes were needed. when we reform, we follow the rules in force in the eu and the member states. the mechanism of budgetary linkage to rule of law violations (violation of values referred to in article 2 teu) should be permanently removed from the draft regulation. it duplicates the mechanism under article 7 teu by marginalizing the role of the eu council and the european council in the process of assessing a breach of the rule of law by a member state, and deprives the article 7 procedure of its multi-stage character, thus infringing the law of the member state addressed. the introduction of a budgetary and rule of law mechanism separate from article 7 teu is not based on the treaty. the commission notes that the commission has not provided any information on the number of cases of non-compliance with the requirements of the regulation. poland also opposed the mandate of the presidency to open negotiations with the ep on the basis of this draft.
in writing. i am not at all pleased that we are in a situation where we are forced to discuss the linking of payments of eu funds to the rule of law by the member states. compliance with that principle should be self-evident and natural for the member states. the european union is not just a common market, it is also a set of common principles and values. even if we were still at the earliest stage of integration, at the stage of the common market, respect for the rule of law, which builds legal certainty and trust, would be essential. let us also emphasize that this principle is not a matter of theory, it is ultimately a denial of the right of individuals to liberty, security, access to an independent court. but since the anti-democratic actions of some governments have forced us to discuss and work on the appropriate legislation in this area, i would like to emphasize strongly that there is no place in the european union for breaking the rule of law and we must do everything to prevent it from happening. and to do so in a way that the consequences are not borne by eu citizens, but by undemocratic governments. i therefore consider that the disbursement of the funds should be resumed immediately once the breach of the rule of law has ceased. i also support a mechanism that ensures that the final beneficiaries, such as ngos and local governments, are paid, without central governments breaking the rule of law.
in writing. we welcomed the progress of the legislative work in the council on the draft regulation establishing a budgetary conditionality mechanism. however, the compromise reached by the member states diverges significantly from the position adopted by the european parliament at first reading. first, the council narrows down the application of the regulation by combining respect for the rule of law with the protection of the eu's financial interests. this may seem somewhat justified in the context of opinions suggesting an unacceptable duplication of the rule of law mechanism in the treaty in the ep and council regulation. it should be noted, however, that article 7 teu has proved to be wholly ineffective. this is a fundamental problem which threatens to destroy the union in the long run. i therefore believe that as the european parliament we should strive to protect more effectively all the values enshrined in article 2 teu. our voice cannot be ignored by the member states in the council, even though in today's world the establishment of a general budgetary conditionality mechanism is a real challenge both politically and legally. we cannot simply accept the compromise of the german presidency and we must look for solutions that go further. i hope that parliament will continue to take a principled position on the regulation in question and seek to modify it in line with the position adopted at first reading. the reintroduction of the reverse qualified majority voting method in the council for the implementation of sanctions and the effective protection of final beneficiaries of union funds are critical issues.
in writing. the principle of equality between women and men is today the basic standard of human and civil rights. in poland, this principle is regulated by law and constitutionally protected. it is also clear that increasing the representation of women in the highest decision-making bodies of listed companies is an important objective. however, an analysis of the consequences of the implementation of the provisions of the proposed directive calls into question their usefulness in achieving that equality, and the imposition of rigid parity standards on commercial law practitioners may have the opposite effect. it may lead to a situation where the level of motivation among women entrepreneurs is reduced due to the expectation of preferential treatment. the so-called 'golden skirt' phenomenon may also emerge, whereby a small number of women participate simultaneously in the supervisory boards and management boards of many companies, with the result that the participation of women in the highest decision-making bodies of companies does not increase. the aim of the directive is not to improve the status and position of women, but to express an ideological feminist view. equally important, the project is contrary to the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality as set out in article 5 (3) of the treaty on european union. finally, it is worth noting that the imposition of female representation by the principle of parity in advance diminishes the value of candidates and is contrary to the elementary sense of justice and dignity.

executive vice-president of the commission. – madam president, i see that many people who’ve made comments have left, but still, i’ll try and answer more in general to some of the comments that were made. first of all, to those people mostly sitting here, who are always referring to the citizens to not be ambitious. well, if there’s one thing that’s consistent over the last year – even in the middle of the pandemic – a large majority of our citizens want us to act to face the climate crisis. it is the citizens who are asking this of us: even in the middle of the pandemic, when they’re very much worried about their health, when they are very much worried about their jobs, they still see the climate crisis as something they want us to act upon. secondly, in the same context, don’t come at me with ‘sovereignty – we need to do it at the national level’. our citizens understand this is a problem we can only tackle on a global level, and that europe needs to take the leadership as europe. individual member states can no longer do that. another remark in reaction to some of the criticisms: the costs. it’s expensive. well, let me be very clear. if you look at our impact assessment, and to put it in layman’s terms: this is going to be bloody hard to do! it is hard to do, and we will ask sacrifice of everyone – industry, our citizens, the transport system, etc. it’s a tough job, but it can be done, and the sooner we start, the lower the cost. the sooner we start, the earlier the benefits. that’s why we had our target of -55% for 2030. so we shouldn’t hide the fact that this is going to be, as i said, bloody difficult to do – but just imagine for one second the cost of non-action. how are you going to go to a small town, such as limone piemonte, where they’ve just suffered the most horrible weather conditions and people have died and the village is a shambles, and tell them: no, it’s too costly, we won’t do this. what’s the cost of that? what’s the cost of another monthly gota fria in valencia if we don’t do something about that? what’s the cost if people are saying: here, we should keep all these coal mines open, but there’s no market for the coal – what’s the cost of keeping people in jobs that have no future? the cost is huge. we need to help people find new jobs, retrain them – but show solidarity. that’s why just transition is essential. without just transition there will just be no transition and we will never get to our -55% goal. now of course, on the other side of the chamber, you want a higher target. i maintain that -55 is difficult but feasible. i also maintain it is in line with our international obligations. i say this with force, because i do not like the argument that we should be doing more because other industrialised nations are doing less. we should be leading but also taking others along the way. i am quite sure that xi jinping saying that china will be carbon-neutral by 2060 is a consequence of what we’re doing, and we need to convince others. the fact that south africa has now said: ‘we want to be climate-neutral by 2050’ – that’s huge for a country like south africa. let’s use that and create more international cooperation, and then -55, i think, is very important. a final point on using carbon sink. look at the state of our forests. look at what’s happening with biodiversity in europe. if we continue like this, there will be no pollinators anymore. how are you going to explain that to the farmers when they say: ‘let’s keep the present agricultural policy’? there will be no agriculture if there are no pollinators. there will be no agriculture if there’s no water for the land. there will be no agriculture if a storm sweeps away the topsoil every time. and we need to look after our forests. carbon sink is diminishing in europe. we need to increase it. we need to look after the situation of our grasslands, our peatlands, our forests, and in that context, i believe it is wise to include carbon sink in our targets and to make sure we increase the health of our natural environment.

the debate is closed. the vote on the amendments will take place shortly and the final vote in the afternoon of wednesday, 7 october 2020. written statements (rule 171)
in writing. european climate law is a legal act that sets the path for the european union to achieve full climate neutrality by 2050 at the latest. it's not an easy process. many are concerned about the competitiveness of our companies, the preservation of jobs and the possible rise in the prices of products and services. this is a particular challenge for poland, given the very high share of coal in electricity and heat production. but a radical reduction in greenhouse gas emissions is absolutely necessary to stop climate catastrophe. it's no longer a question of whether, but when and how to achieve that goal. there is no doubt that the fight against climate change today must be fought on many fronts, and climate neutrality will not be achieved by european climate law alone. the european commission has already announced, among other things, the revision and expansion of the eu's greenhouse gas emissions trading scheme, the tightening of carbon emission standards for road vehicles, further support for the development of electromobility, and the improvement of energy efficiency and renewable energy policies. these actions are necessary to decarbonise the european economy. however, adequate financial support for example through the eu's cohesion policy and the just transformation fund is equally important. only then can we reconcile climate protection with the socio-economic challenges we face today.
in writing. european climate law is one of the flagship elements of the european green deal and as such should be characterised as the highest legislative standard. i have some reservations about the envi report. first, the impact assessment of this proposal is not sufficient it should cover both the eu as a whole and the member states, and include specific data on the impact of the increased target on individual sectors. secondly, the trajectory being set by one institution alone, the european commission, without a wider consultation of stakeholders and member state governments, raises serious doubts. thirdly, as a member of the agri committee in the european parliament, i do not support the introduction of a climate-related greenhouse budget, which would burden all sectors, including the agricultural sector. farmers will be burdened not only by the new ecological requirements of the farm to fork strategy and the biodiversity strategy, but also by greenhouse gas emissions requirements. we must not forget that agriculture is a carbon emitter, but also a significant carbon sink. this role must be emphasised at every step if we do not want excessive demands to force farmers to stop production. for the reasons mentioned above, i voted against the report on european climate law.
in writing. floods, droughts, tornadoes, extreme heat, rising sea and ocean levels, species extinction, famine, forced migration and epidemics. these are just some of the effects of the climate crisis. decades of ruthless exploitation of the planet's resources have brought us to the brink of collapse. many of the losses we have suffered are irreversible, but we can and must take steps to save the earth and its people from disaster. according to a unep report published in 2019, achieving the 1.5°c target of the paris agreement as the desired state will require the eu to reduce emissions by at least 65% by 2030. scientific studies clearly show that the effects of an increase in average temperature of even 0.5°c above 1.5°c would be incomparably more severe. in the first case, it is estimated that about 37% of the population will be exposed to extreme temperatures once every 5 years, and in the second case, it is 14%. a 2°c rise in temperature would also mean the loss of about 99% of coral reefs and a rise in sea level of 0.46 m. the stakes are high. it is therefore important that the eu does not compromise and follows the current scientific knowledge, which is clear in this area. an ambitious 2030 reduction target is necessary and we need to start implementing it today.

in writing. the types of digital services and the roles of digital service providers have changed significantly since the e-commerce directive was adopted 20 years ago. in the changed circumstances, member states have started to define network services differently (e.g. netzdg in germany, french law on illegal online content, etc.) and this would inevitably lead to the fragmentation of the eu single market. it is therefore essential to modernise the definition of network services. the main elements of the e-commerce directive, namely the principle of limited liability, the principle of country of establishment (coo) and the principle of non-general monitoring obligation, should certainly be preserved in the context of the transposition. regulation of digital services should not impose disproportionate new obligations on undertakings. nor should regulation be a hindrance to innovation. i am categorically opposed to the banning of the use of ai-based facial recognition systems by the public sector. we have to protect people's privacy, but we can't kill innovation. i don't think it's wise to ban targeted advertising. as a consumer, i prefer to be informed about goods and services that are of real interest to me, rather than being drowned out by the noise of advertising. it was with a heavy heart that i supported the compromise.
in writing. artificial intelligence is a very difficult topic from a legal point of view. it must be made clear that we cannot accept a state in which decision-making is completely independent of man. artificial intelligence comes with a lot of convenience, it makes our lives easier, it helps, no doubt, but it cannot be responsible. all processes based on it, their design and creation must always be the responsibility of man. there can be no question of any transfer of state authority to machines.
in writing. the digital services code is an initiative that aims to improve the functioning of the single market for digital services. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 concerning the conditions for the participation of the republic of moldova in the union programme 'horizon 2020 - the framework programme for research and innovation (2014-2020) '. in addition to market improvements, it will be equally important to increase network security and protect the fundamental rights of internet users, and to establish effective market surveillance for the moderation of illegal content by intermediaries. in today's world of widespread access to online content, there is a need for transparent tools to notify platforms and appeal their decisions. the current rules and practices are not consistent, which is to a large extent to the detriment of users and is causing chaos in the single market. another important element is to ensure the security of all network users by preventing and combating cybercrime. the key issue will be to improve cooperation between online platforms and the competent law enforcement authorities in the individual member states, while maintaining the highest guarantees in the field of fundamental rights. there is a need to create an effective mechanism to separate illegal content from content that is legal but harmful or misinformative. dsa must be a future-proof solution that provides security and legal certainty to all digital market users.
the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the member states unanimously agreed to pursue a common security and defence policy by incorporating it into the treaty. strategies have been drawn up, agencies and instruments have been set up, defence funds have been set up. the question today is, are they effective? with each conflict in the union's neighbourhood, we become more aware of our dependence and almost vulnerability in the face of a potential threat. this is a step forward, but it's too small to say that we're actually able to make ourselves safe in our environment. in recent years, conventional threats have been joined by hybrid conflicts such as cyberattacks, disinformation and economic pressure. and then there are global challenges: climate change and pandemics. we realized that europe had to have an impact on the order in its region. our soft power must be complemented by hard power. the european union needs a common security and defence policy for its own security, for the stabilisation of its neighbourhood. those who today, including in my country, are shouting so loudly about national sovereignty, do not see or ignore our dependence on security. it's time to build a greater responsibility for our own security, not in opposition to nato, but alongside and in support of nato. however, the compromise reached on pesco has revealed the extent to which political rhetoric is not linked to military reality. political narratives of european strategic autonomy clash with the reality of a glaring lack of military capabilities and the current uncertainty about the us military presence on the continent. so what is pesco? the permanent cooperation in the field of security, as described in the treaty of lisbon over a decade ago, was only established in practice in 2017. it is a form of military and defence cooperation in which 25 member states, including poland, currently participate. it is based on two pillars: the implementation of 20 commitments and the joint implementation of projects. the main recommendations in my report are to call on participating member states to move from national defence priorities to a european approach, as no member state is able to address the current threats on its own. pesco was originally conceived as an avant-garde concept, involving the most advanced and ambitious member states in the field of defence. the participation of 25 countries means that pesco is not a cooperation of leaders. we urge that the covid-19 pandemic does not lead to national defense budget cuts, as paradoxically, military spending can increase readiness for the next pandemic. several of the pesco projects currently underway, such as military mobility and european medical command, would enhance our capacity to take collective action in a pandemic. we also recommend that consideration be given to the inclusion in pesco of the eu battle group system, which clearly needs reform. we suggest that this could increase its operational capacity and efficiency by creating permanent multinational units used for military or crisis management tasks. instead of merging a brigade with national battalions, a european brigade should be composed of volunteers from member states and be financed from a common budget and be subject to the foreign affairs council. finally, we call for the immediate adoption of a decision governing future cooperation with third countries under pesco.

in writing. in the face of the global coronavirus pandemic, we urgently need a new common agricultural policy that will provide food security and financial support for over 10 million farms in the eu. high quality and healthy food for 500 million europeans means efficient, financially stable and innovative agriculture! that is why direct payments under the european agricultural guarantee fund are so important. i do not agree that the distribution of funds between the individual eu countries is still unfair and unfair to farmers in some member states, including poland. the slow pace of alignment of the level of direct payments proposed by the commission maintains the disparities in support for agricultural producers operating in the single market, which are inconsistent with the new cap objectives. i agree with the need to increase the environmental and climate ambition of the cap. however, i am opposed to setting minimum levels of budgetary expenditure for eco-schemes. in my view, the approach that is more appropriate and effective is one in which the member states decide how, by what means and in what proportion these objectives are to be achieved. i also believe that member states should be given flexibility to use the unused funds for the year for eco-schemes. i believe we can reach an agreement quickly that is fair and equitable for all european farmers.

in writing. the importance of protecting european and global forests is undeniable. however, this report is not fit for purpose, goes beyond the eu legal framework and disproportionately endangers the functioning of european smes. without an impact assessment, the proposal would list the products most often associated by green ngos with deforestation and the degradation of natural ecosystems. the left would also leave open the possibility of extending the scope of the regulation. without a european certification system, the process would be completely opaque and disproportionate. the arbitrary nature of the report is also problematic. the rapporteur would extend the proposal to all economic operators and the entire value chain. this would have unforeseeable consequences and would impose an administrative burden on smes. in addition, the document thus touches on a number of areas of member states' competence, which is also unacceptable. the protection of forests should not be promoted by listing and quotas at either european or global level. we need positive incentives and international cooperation. in doing so, it is also appropriate to take into account the best practices of the member states. one such example is hungary, which has committed to increasing its forest cover by a third to 27% by 2030.
in writing. – global preservation of forests and preventing their degradation are some of the biggest sustainability challenges of our times, without which the objectives of the 2030 agenda for sustainable development, the paris agreement and the green deal cannot be achieved. i welcome the creation of a forest observatory to collect data and information on deforestation in europe as well as globally. we have to call for this observatory to establish a mechanism to protect forest defenders. i fully support the creating of the early-warning alert mechanisms in order to notify public authorities, companies, including third-party schemes, and consumers of commodities originating in areas of eco-system conversion risk concerning loss and deterioration of forest and savannah and areas where human rights have been violated, and to assist in tackling these issues by intensifying dialogue and data sharing with respective third countries. this mechanism is important to preserve the forestry sector which employs at least 500 000 people directly in the union, and 13 million people worldwide, especially in rural areas. it encourages the commission to strengthen the eu action plan on flegt, with a focus on voluntary partnership agreements, and incorporate it into the new european forest strategy to encourage third countries to abandon deforestation policies.

funding aspects needed for the achievement of gender equality in eu foreign and security policy. in light of the current global challenges, like the climate emergency and growing trends towards authoritarianism, where women and girls are the most impacted, the need for a gender-based eu foreign and security policy becomes more urgent than ever. following the example of a number of countries, member of the commission. – mr president, i am honoured to present to you today the state of the energy union report. every year, it’s an opportunity to take stock of our energy policy and assess whether we are on track with implementing the energy union. the 2020 report is the first one since we launched our new sustainability and growth strategy, the european green deal. a well-functioning energy union is the necessary basis to deliver our climate commitment by 2050. together with this report, i presented three key initiatives on 14 october: the renovation wave, the methane strategy and the commission recommendations on energy poverty. the initiatives of the 14 october energy package are important stepping stones to reach our 2030 climate target plan. they will make sure that we seize the significant decarbonisation potential of buildings and address energy poverty in order not to leave anybody behind in the clean energy transition. national energy and climate plans (necps) will also remain an important tool in achieving the minimum 55% reduction in greenhouse gases. together with the state of the energy union, we also published a detailed assessment of the plans of each member state. the final necps are complete, robust and ambitious. our analysis shows that each member state still has some work to do, especially on energy efficiency. but overall we are heading in the right direction and the plans demonstrate that europe can meet ambitious climate targets. the commission will ensure a clear and inclusive follow—up of those plans, including on the progress of implementation and the need to revise the level of ambition of necps to reflect a higher carbon emission reduction target for 2030. let me now go back to the state of the energy union report. this report provides an overview of the progress of the energy union across all its dimensions. i would like to focus on three areas today. first, we know that delivering the higher climate ambition in the energy sector is a genuine investment challenge. the state of the energy union report maps out the funding opportunities offered by the recovery and resilience facility and other eu instruments. in particular, the annual sustainable growth strategy identified three energy-related flagships – clean energy technologies, renovation and sustainable transport – where member states can focus their national renovation plans. this shows that next generation eu offers an unprecedented opportunity to mobilise resources to promote the clean and digital transformation of our economies, and we should use it. the report, however, shows that national budgets devote a declining share to clean energy research and innovation. when we measure the volumes of research funding as a share of gdp, europe has one of the lowest rates among the major global players. private sector investment in energy union r&t priorities is also slowing down and i’m very concerned by this trend. second, the report shows that the volume of energy subsidies, in particular for fossil fuels, is still considerable. fossil fuel subsidies amounted to eur 50 billion in the eu in 2018. this is one third of all our energy subsidies. the european green deal is clear: fossil fuel subsidies have to end. they remain a major impediment to a cost-efficient energy and climate transition, but also to a functioning internal market. therefore, the commission will reinforce its cooperation with member states to phase out fossil fuel subsidies and reduce fossil fuel consumption. energy subsidies should be targeted to boost the uptake of new energy technologies, to promote sustainable patterns of energy consumption, and to lower energy bills. third, this year’s state of the energy union included for the first time a report on the competitiveness of the clean energy industry in europe. the findings are quite significant. the growth of the clean energy technology sector has significantly outpaced that of the conventional energy sector. clean energy technologies have created more jobs and added more to gross domestic product and labour productivity. this has been especially obvious in energy efficiency, where the number of jobs went up 17.4% between 2000 and 2017. the competitiveness report also shows that eu industry holds a strong global position in some of the key technologies, namely offshore solar energy storage, batteries and hydrogen technologies, which have a major scaling-up potential over the coming years. in the coming months, we will take these elements forward and we will focus in our discussions with all relevant stakeholders on a value-chain-based approach to support our industries and innovators in the eu to maintain or achieve global success. i will stop here and now i will take your questions.

president. - emergency laws and regulations restricting the fundamental rights of citizens should only be used in genuine emergencies, such as war and other serious crises. is there a real emergency in the eu? covid-19 is a relatively mild virus that has only been able to lead to a crisis because the capacity of health care has not been calculated for pandemics and governments are insufficiently prepared to manage a crisis. as a result, unfortunately, more intervention is now needed than would have been necessary with proper emergency preparation. to prevent history from repeating itself, action must be taken not only within governments but also within the eu institutions. the next crisis could be a pandemic, but it could also be a severe recession, social unrest or even war. governments should take this into account when formulating policies and budgets and build in emergency buffers so that in the future we rarely or never have to rely on emergency interventions, since true emergencies fortunately rarely occur.

the rapporteur. madam president, as someone who is familiar with this subject, commissioner reynders, and my colleagues, i am pleased to be starting this debate with you this morning, but above all because i have been able to wage a noble fight for better consumer protection for the last two and a half years. why was this directive created? scandals as big as dieselgate and the unjustified cancellation of flights by ryanair had convinced the european commission, as we remember, to legislate, presenting a draft directive. it was april 11, 2018. two and a half years later, after many meetings and negotiations and many compromises and, let us say, twists and turns, here we are all together today in a position to offer a new, concrete right to european citizens: the right to associate themselves to obtain redress if they suffer damage as a result of the illegal practice of a multinational. until now, we knew that, when faced with airlines, large banks or large industrial companies, a consumer alone would not take legal action, because legal action is a long, costly and uncertain process. until now, these class actions were only possible in some european countries: about 10 states did not have them and, above all, it was impossible to bring an action in another country and thus join other european consumers. with this european-wide collective action, we are therefore proposing a change in ambition and a change in dimension to all citizens of the european union. this result is the result of long struggles to get each political group to agree to step out of its ideological comfort zone. everyone understood that we all had a lot to gain from finding a balanced solution which would both be more protective of consumers and, i repeat, sufficiently safe for the life of businesses, which need it. nothing was gained in advance, because many preconceived ideas were conveyed and dictated by seemingly contradictory and often traditional interests which had to be accepted to be pushed in the face of new requirements. i would like to thank each political group, without exception, for finding the way to unity and reaching a solution which, i say, parliament can be proud of. it is precisely this balance that we have also been able to impose at the trilogue meetings and which ultimately gives all its strength to this reform. everyone wins, the consumer first. the full compensation will be paid to him, unlike the deviations of the american system, which we did not want. whether it is the user of a washing machine, a financial product, a website or an airline, these class actions will enable every european consumer who has been harmed to be better defended, better compensated and ultimately better protected. companies also benefit: they will be protected from abusive or defamatory delaying actions by a significant number of conditions that we have required and which will guarantee the transparency of funding and the absence of conflicts of interest of qualified entities. for example, hedge funds and law firms will not be able to bring legal proceedings and be parties to legal proceedings themselves, as only authorised and recognised consumer associations will be able to do so. europe is finally winning, at a time when people are accusing the european union, sometimes rightly, of imposing many standards and constraints. it shows that it is able to adapt to new needs and, above all, that it is able to offer new rights to citizens. this is economic progress, legal progress, but above all political progress which we must all embrace and which we can all claim. i would like to thank the european commission, and in particular commissioner reynders, but also all his teams who have worked so hard. i would like to hope, by the largest possible majority, this reform will become an important reform of this mandate, but above all a strong added value of europe in the daily lives of its citizens.

member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, let me thank you for the opportunity this morning to discuss the directive on representative actions. i would first of all like to thank mr geoffroy didier and the non-existent rapporteurs of the committee on legal affairs, but also all the actors involved in the european parliament, in particular the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, for their work during the interinstitutional negotiations, especially as the work was carried out under difficult conditions during the croatian presidency in view of the lockdown. the representative actions directive is the european union's operational response to violations of consumer rights. the latter are often helpless against certain professionals who resort to illegal business practices. we all have dieselgate in our minds, to name just one example. the situation created by the covid-19 pandemic has further highlighted the difficulties faced by consumers who wish to assert their rights. i am thinking here of the mass cancellations of flights and package tours without respect for the right to reimbursement: we spoke about this again last night during our debates on the consumer agenda and on mr david cormand's report. the adoption of this directive is therefore more necessary than ever. it will enable all european consumers to have at their disposal, finally, this powerful tool for protecting their rights, which is the collective redress. the text agreed by the co-legislators is balanced, whether it concerns the operation of the system, the control of the financing of representative actions to avoid conflicts of interest, support for qualified entities to ensure the efficiency of the procedure or the various guarantees linked to the cost of the representative action in compensation. the scope of the text is sufficiently broad to cover violations of consumer rights in a wide variety of areas, far beyond the traditional scope of consumer protection. these include energy, telecommunications, data protection, financial services and medical devices. the procedural arrangements provided for are such as to ensure the effectiveness of the mechanism, while respecting the procedural autonomy of the member states. the directive also provides important safeguards for professionals at all levels of the procedure. the text thus ensures that their right of defence is respected and the risk of unfair litigation is avoided. i would like to thank the european parliament again for its strong commitment to consumers throughout this process. we can welcome this great success, which will help european consumers to assert their rights in an effective way.

on behalf of the id group. madam president, union is strength: this adage is particularly true in consumer law. when consumers are victimized by a big company, they often feel helpless to assert their rights. this directive aims to help them obtain justice by providing them with a european collective action mechanism. the directive requires each member state to designate qualified non-profit-making bodies which will be responsible for bringing legal proceedings before national courts on behalf of consumers who have suffered harm. these qualified entities will therefore have the merit of breaking the loneliness of consumers by bringing them together in collective actions, thus transforming their initial weakness into strength. the directive is flexible in that it allows each state to choose both associations and public bodies. in addition, it respects national collective action systems where they already exist, as is the case in france since the law of 17 march 2014. if successful, the class action will oblige the company to offer the consumers who have been injured the most appropriate form of compensation: compensation, repair, replacement, price reduction, termination of the contract or refund of the price paid. this new mechanism is therefore a major step forward for consumer protection, as it will make it possible to repair, more effectively than today, the serial damage caused by large companies such as that caused by volkswagen in the dieselgate scandal.
i have to say, madam president, five years ago, a historic environmental and consumer scandal came to light. volkswagen had installed multi-million dollar fraud software in their cars to make it look like the cars were more environmentally friendly than they actually were. i mention this case now because in many ways it is the backdrop for the legislation we are about to adopt. the dieselgate scandal was a scandal in itself, but it also made it clear that we had a hole in the european union's legal system. consumers were not able to bring a collective action in germany but had to do so nationally in their own countries. of course, this should not be the case. the single market must not only benefit businesses, it must also benefit consumers. there is a need to ensure effective legal protection when companies cheat. i am therefore also pleased that an agreement on collective action for european consumers has been reached. the more consumers who stand together behind a lawsuit, the stronger they will be in court. not everything in this agreement is perfect, but i think it is important to be happy about it, and i would like to emphasize two things. one is that it is good that the principle of the loser pays has finally been introduced. large class action lawsuits are often very expensive and therefore it is only reasonable that the losing party should pay. secondly, i am very pleased that we are going to have a european consumer ombudsman. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the consumer is not discriminated against. i do not think that this will necessarily prevent a new dieselgate scandal, but it will give consumers better opportunities to defend their rights collectively in the event of being let down by companies again. so i support the legislation, even if there are a few weaknesses in it.
i have to say, madam president, the system of collective actions is not a system historically rooted in european law. the system comes from the anglican case law, as we know. in europe, where roman law has been adopted, there is therefore - at least in continental europe - nowhere a similar legal system. as a lawyer, of course, you are very skeptical about this. of course, it is not known whether this can also result in a meaningful integration at the end of the day and at the end of this implementation. but as far as the matter of collective actions is concerned, i can say for myself that i think it is quite sensible to incorporate them, because it is primarily in the interests of the consumer. we have a very balanced situation here. on the one hand we have consumers, whose market power is rather small, and on the other hand large companies, which have great market power, and therefore, of course, sufficient capital to fight any legal disputes. i therefore think that this should be implemented. the optin system is important, which means that a complaint can only be lodged if the person concerned has a mandate to do so.
i'm not going to let you get away with this. it is good news that we are discussing today the completion of the directive on representative actions and the possibility of collective redress for consumers in all member states. the adoption of this law is important and is expected by thousands of union citizens, as the experience of recent years shows that collective infringements of consumer rights continue to occur in many member states, mainly through misleading, aggressive marketing or other unlawful commercial practices. in poland, where i am a member of parliament, there has been a recent case of mass consumer rights violations involving the unfair granting of mortgage loans indexed to foreign currency or the frequent practice of selling products of inferior quality. these operations have affected thousands of citizens and have often been the cause of human tragedy and misery. in this context, i believe that the european parliament should strongly support the solutions provided for in this directive, as they will make a significant contribution to improving the level of protection of consumer rights. they will also ensure the efficiency of the procedures by applying the urgency procedure and avoid a situation where high legal costs could become an obstacle to collective enforcement of consumer rights.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank honourable members very much for their interventions and for this interesting debate. i will first reply on the comments addressed to the commission. this commission does everything to support an independent, professional and trustworthy media because, more than ever before, we need objective news which will inform citizens about the situation. we have to do it and we are doing everything with the competences we have. concrete steps on the concrete situation is always a matter of a thorough analysis as to whether this is against eu rules and whether we have the instruments to take concrete steps which will address an individual case. you know the system very well. we work on individual cases, which can be addressed by enquiry into infringements – which is not this case – and we can work by adopting new legislation, or proposing new legislation, to address systemic issues. this is what we are doing. we now have the audiovisual media services directive already being transposed into national laws. we are scrutinising whether it is done in full because, if not, we have to launch an infringement against the member state and ask for an improvement in the implementation or application of the european directive in national law. this is now ongoing because this directive came into force this year. we are preparing very thoroughly for the application date of the copyright directive, which will come next year in june. it will be a very important moment in history for strengthening the position of professional journalism because, behind this heavily lobbied piece of legislation – i think you will remember the time when this was in the final stage of adoption – there was a very simple idea, namely that professional journalists have to get paid for their work. this is going to come into force next year in june and the commission is prepared to help with proper implementation in the member states, which will not be possible to circumvent. we have already seen in france that an effort was made by google to find some middle way solution, and we said no. it has to be implemented and applied in full. we are going to adopt the european democracy action plan and the media action plan next week, on 2 december. i will not go into details because of the time limit here, but you will see that in everything we are doing – by the current legislation which is already in application or the rules we are going to adopt – we are trying to strengthen the position of independent media because we need the independent and professional media to be strong and do their job. the character of their job is twofold. one is that they are economic actors. what we see now, in the time of covid, is the more we need professional and objective media, the less money they get. they are in horrible financial distress now in the time of covid. that’s why we recommended to the member states to use the state aid schemes also to help the media as economic players and employers. the second task of the media, and an indispensable role, is that they must remain strong watchdogs of democracy. they must hold us, who are in power, under control. we are also working in this direction. you will see in the european democracy action plan that we will propose several actions to strengthen their position as the watchdogs of democracy. i will always emphasise professional independent trustworthy media. this is what we are speaking about. and why? why are we trying to strengthen the position of the media? because we see clearly that when the media are weak, they are easy targets for political and economic pressure. this is what we see in europe. the trend is worsening. in the summer this year, we published the media pluralism monitor, where we saw this very clearly. a worsening trend of political pressure on the media has increased everywhere in europe. economic pressure, now made more dramatic by the impact of covid, has made the situation of the media very difficult. advertisers have moved to the online sphere and 50% of all advertising money goes to facebook and google in europe. this is the reality. when the media are hungry, then they have no other choice than to take the money from those who want to impose the political agenda. this is what we are witnessing in many cases. so we need to do everything we can – this is for me a systemic measure – to make the media stronger and not to be driven into this financial trap because they of course need to make money doing their job. we have a very vivid dialogue with media organisations because we also want the eu money to help, but of course we cannot pay individual media because we have to respect the independence of the media. i will finish by asking all of us to try to look at things objectively. the eu is, of course, supporting the media, which is also financed by foreign actors when they operate as business players. but when we see that there is a political agenda behind that, then there is something wrong. thank you very much for this debate. i do not believe that this was the last debate about the media. this was a geographically—specific one, but it also revealed the systemic issues we are facing and that we are trying to solve at european union level because we have a limit to systemic functioning solutions, including the increase in transparency of ownership. this is one of the things which we now want to scrutinise in more depth because this is one of the conditions which are already in the audiovisual media services directive, which is now in force.
the debate is closed.

in writing. the treaty of lisbon gives legal force to the charter of fundamental rights. the charter has been accepted by all eu countries except the united kingdom and poland, which have reserved the limitation of its protection for their citizens by the provisions of protocol 7, known as the uk protocol. article 1 makes it clear that, for the avoidance of doubt, nothing in title iv of the charter creates rights which can be enforced by judicial means applicable to poland, except where poland has provided for such rights in its national law. article 2: where a provision of the charter relates to national law or practice, it shall apply to poland only to the extent that the rights and principles contained in that provision are recognised by polish law or practice. on the basis of these two articles, poland is sovereign in the matters raised in today's debate. we do not agree to impose on poles how they should act or think in matters where they have their inalienable rights. the constitution of the republic of poland protects every life, the life of the mother, but also the unborn. poles are a wise nation that can solve its own internal problems and does not need pressure from the eu institutions, because that is the only way to see this vote. today's resolution exceeds all democratic standards and its provisions are a call to violate polish and international law.

mr president, any pharmaceutical strategy must meet two fundamental requirements. the first requirement: the importance of the public sector, universities and public laboratories in the research and development of vaccines and new medicines, the need to challenge the hegemony of the pharmaceutical multinationals, to ensure the primacy of the public interest over business. covid has made particularly visible the perversity of the prominence given to multinationals in the acquisition of vaccines still in development. public money is used to finance research, to pay for the purchase of vaccines and, finally, to relieve companies of obligations relating to the conditions of supply of products and to alleviate the risks arising from their use. the second requirement is that we must consider national strategies to ensure that each country has sovereignty in this area, that we must recognize the right of each country to produce, and the need to produce, of course, within the framework of the necessary international cooperation in this area. this is particularly important in the case of countries such as portugal, which are very dependent in this area. the right to produce and the pharmaceutical industry cannot be an exclusive right of only a few countries.

i would like to congratulate the commission on the publication of the new european pharmaceutical strategy. the pandemic has raised many issues and raised many questions. one of them is the growing disparity between member states in the quality of healthcare. the new pharmaceutical strategy is a good foundation for the radical changes that lie ahead, but there are aspects that it has not sufficiently identified. for example, by 2050, the world's population will grow to 9 billion. it will be difficult to provide adequate health care if the health professions and their related disciplines and institutions do not work together, and preventive medicine will be extremely important. i think that strategy needs to play a much more important role in this aspect, and that it needs to be more actively involved in developing and promoting healthy lifestyle habits, rather than being focused solely on treating disease. the second aspect concerns the impact of climate change on quality of life and health. loss of biodiversity, air pollution, and global warming are adding to the number of new infectious diseases. ignoring the link between climate change and pandemics would be a dangerous mistake.
mr president, first of all i would like to say that i am not a big fan of widespread government regulation of the economy. in my opinion, markets are far more productive if they are competitive. however, when it comes to critical infrastructure markets, one has to admit that they cannot be left unsupervised. the european market for pharmaceutical products is one such market. the pandemic has proven that it needs more regulation and coordination so that patients receive the best possible access to medicines and medical treatments. for this reason, i welcome the new pharmaceutical strategy, which the commission adopted yesterday. i especially welcome proposals for actions aimed at increasing the accessibility of medicines for the treatment of childhood cancer or rare diseases. this has not been a priority for producers so far. i’m looking forward, and committed, to working with the commission and other actors on the implementation of the strategy in order to achieve higher standards of healthcare and to protect citizens’ well—being.
mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to leave. europe and the world are fighting covid-19, and this fight has taught us all that we really don't stand a chance against global challenges like covid or other challenges and the new fight we're on the verge of. this is a fight for cancer patients. unfortunately, in the coming months, millions of patients with cancer that is too late to be diagnosed, often advanced, probably metastatic, and sometimes terminal, will be coming to european hospitals, because covid is delaying treatment, delaying diagnosis, delaying care. we must therefore make a strategic decision today, commissioner, to build a system of continuity of supply of cancer medicines. what we need to do today is build a strategic inventory of cancer drugs, critical cancer drugs, that we can use to help patients. the second challenge that we face today, after the covid experience, is to build a robust system to respond to critical and emergency situations. a system of information sharing between governments and joint response in the form of buying medicines and securing equipment must be built up as quickly as possible. these two challenges - the strategic stockpiling of medicines in europe and the emergency response system - are the biggest challenges facing us today, the commissioner and the whole of europe.

in writing. the agreement on drinking water quality is an important achievement. in its new form, the directive is not only about water security, but also about access to it, which is a major issue, especially in the context of climate change. it introduces concrete solutions to reconcile and combine these two objectives. regulations on risk analysis, materials used, parameters of harmful substances take account of new realities and threats. the emphasis on providing drinking water and on ensuring access to it for disadvantaged groups is to be appreciated. however, if we look at the different solutions in the context of the second document on the implementation of eu water legislation under discussion today, we can ask whether we are not taking a step too far in the right direction: whether, in pushing for ideologically sound solutions, we are not ignoring the realities and costs - both immediate and long-term economic and social costs. ensuring access to safe drinking water is a priority, as is concern for the environment. however, its implementation must take account of the needs of the economy, especially agriculture, which will bear the costs of overly restrictive rules. the question is, how will the various regulations affect the functioning of agriculture and industry?
in writing. according to the european environment agency report (no 7/2018 entitled european waters assessment of status and pressures 2018), only 40% of all surface waters in europe are in good condition or have an adequate ecological potential, and only 38% are in a chemical equilibrium. i welcome the eu member states' intensive efforts to improve water quality and meet the high standards of eu water legislation. however, it should be stressed that the system of environmental performance indicators proposed by the european parliament should accurately reflect actual progress in improving surface water quality and provide a broader understanding of some definitions, taking into account the biodiversity and natural transformation of the ecosystem according to the one-out-all-out principle and its crucial importance, which unfortunately does not reflect these progresses. as regards the provisions on perfluorinated compounds, a sufficiently cautious approach should be taken to avoid excluding all compounds commonly used in many key industries. i also believe that, in order to reduce disparities in water quality across regions, eu funds should be used appropriately, not only for new investment but also for the maintenance of existing installations, in line with environmental objectives and with the objective of sustainable economic development financed in a manner adapted to the needs.
in writing. we are talking about a very important issue of water quality for human consumption, which affects every person. the proposed directive is another ec step, following the plastics directive, towards a health and safety environment. the issue of revising the directive was raised not only by technological progress but also by the first eu citizens' initiative 'right to water'. access to safe water is a fundamental human right and is also one of the united nations development goals. it is unacceptable that not everyone in europe has access to good quality water. the eu must therefore promote the provision of free, good quality water in public places, perhaps even in every locality. this is what the people of europe want, and this is what they have expressed in their citizens' initiative. the well-being of people must always be our priority, and safe drinking water is our main objective. eu water is of a high standard, but new pollutants, consumer protection and the need to keep up with environmental change need to be taken into account. it is therefore good that the directive has introduced 18 new management parameters. mandatory analysis and risk management are also important. we also need to be vigilant about microplastics, which are becoming the biggest threat to the quality and safety of drinking water. citizens must have full confidence in the quality of their water. we should remember that it is necessary to protect drinking water sources and thus reduce industrial pollution and human behaviour that is not in keeping with the environment.

in writing. the attempt to impose on poland and hungary, and in practice on all eu non-power countries, a system for assessing their rule of law in the absence of any specific criteria, leads to the conclusion that these will be discretionary criteria, each time adapted to the interests of the core eu powers: germany and france. by agreeing to this, these powers can punish governments that go against their will by withdrawing eu funds. it was an instrument to incite the public opinion of the countries thus punished against their governments with the intention of overthrowing them. today such actions are directed against two states, but in the future they may also be directed against greece, spain, italy and others. in principle, a regulation introducing a rule of law clause changes the european union's structure extra-treatyally, and this cannot be allowed.
in writing. it is good that poland and hungary have stopped using open blackmail against partners in the union and withdrawn their vetoes on the multiannual budget for 2021-2027 and the reconstruction fund. this was the only fair way out of the crisis, in accordance with the principle of loyal cooperation between the member states. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a regulation on the budgetary procedure for the financial year 2007-08 and that the council should adopt a regulation on the budgetary procedure for the financial year 2007-08. unfortunately, the conclusions of the european council go far beyond its mandate under the treaties. i consider that the attempt to interfere with the independence of the european commission by requiring it not to propose measures under the budgetary conditionality mechanism until a possible ruling by the court of justice of the european union (since eu law will not be applied until then) and to narrow the scope of the regulation in question of the european parliament and the council clearly infringe the principle of institutional balance. the legal text cannot be changed by conclusions of the european council or by a unilateral declaration by the commission. however, concerns remain that some of the commitments resulting from the european council conclusions will not affect the commission's application of the regulation in a full and effective manner. we should do everything we can to ensure that the commission does not abdicate its role as guardian of the treaties. in this context, it should be recalled that the commission is subject to the political control of parliament, which appoints it and can ultimately dismiss it.
in writing. last week we reached a compromise, bringing to an end the difficult negotiations on the eu budget for the next seven years. this agreement not only gives europeans a guarantee of further economic and economic development of europe, but also an additional €750 billion for post-covid-19 recovery under the next generation eu. the conclusions of the last european council also respect the law of the treaties in the spirit of the sovereignty of the eu member states. the right to decide for ourselves what the future of our countries should be, without being subjected to unjust mechanisms based on discretionary and political criteria. i would like to stress that poland is not and has never been against the efficient and effective use of the eu budget, free from fraud and irregularities, as reflected in the conclusions adopted. i therefore believe that the european parliament and the european commission should fully respect the agreements between the heads of state and government by suspending the application of the cross-compliance regulation until the court of justice of the european union has taken a position and the european commission has developed guidelines in agreement with the member states. i believe this is a huge step towards further building not only a europe that is strong and economically competitive, but also a europe of equality and mutual respect.
in writing. the long negotiations on the eu's financial framework for 2021-2027 have reached an overall compromise. a solution was found to move forward with the adoption of the framework starting next year, despite the manipulative behaviour of poland and hungary, which hampered the adoption and implementation of financial measures. the overall amount of the mff was set at eur 1074.3 billion, with repayment of the budget at eur 1464.3 billion. the focus of the first years of the mfis will be on addressing the health crisis resulting from the covid-19 pandemic and improving the economic situation of member states. it should be noted that the crisis funding will not be provided at the expense of subsequent years. the political compromise covers not only the financial framework but also the future own resources system and the new eu's nextgenerationeu funding. health, agriculture, climate, innovation, social issues and education remain at the heart of funding, and the external dimension of the eu's neighbourhood, development and international cooperation instrument and the solidarity and emergency reserve have been increased.
in writing. – one notes with satisfaction the conclusion of the mff negotiations. we now have a seven—year budgetary framework for the eu. an extra recovery investment programme will enable member states to counter the coronavirus recession. a rule—of—law procedure prevents the allocation of eu funds for purposes that contradict the union’s fundamental values. however, the underlying realities must also be highlighted. these are that: eu decision—making structures are not delivering timely responses to crisis situations; masked by the recovery programme, targets initially set by the european commission and the european parliament as resources needed to carry out the eu’s programme have by far not been reached; the european council and the european parliament diverge totally on how to seek solutions to union challenges, such as on own resources; the european parliament is fuelling the perception that it wants more taxation on citizens – does this improve its political standing?; there has been little real progress in designing rule—of—law evaluative processes that minimise politicisation. rather than a conference on the future of europe, we need an intergovernmental conference to first identify the priorities by which to unlock the most important institutional issues.
in writing. let us clarify two things. first, the european council has no legislative powers. therefore, no political declaration, statement or promise made by the commission has legal force, is a source of law or can be considered as an interpretation of law. the interpretation of the law is the exclusive responsibility of the european court of justice. secondly, the european council, the european commission and the parliament must always exercise particular care and diligence in their public statements on human rights and the rule of law. unfortunately, last week's council position undermined the eu authorities' years of work to strengthen the community's legal system to ensure that member states' governments respect the union's values. the signal that the conditionality mechanism could be frozen until the ecj's ruling was received as a capitulation to the governments of poland and hungary. the council is well aware that such a decision, assuming it was legally binding at all, would delay by as much as two or three years the protection of the rights of eu citizens and the ability of community governments to enforce eu values effectively. the council's view is particularly relevant and poignant in a situation where the governments of poland and hungary have not only not reversed previous decisions targeting judicial freedom, the independence of civil society or the dignity of lgbt+ people, but are taking further political and legal decisions that constitute or may constitute significant violations of our values.

member of the commission. – madam president, it is good to see you again. honourable members, the last five years were the hottest on record, with more frequent heatwaves, droughts and wildfires across europe. temporary drops in greenhouse gas emissions like those caused by the 2008 financial crisis and the current economic disruptions due to the covid—19 pandemic have little effect on the evolution of the planetary climate, and emissions can bounce back quickly. the special report on global warming of 1.5° celsius issued by the intergovernmental panel on climate change demonstrates that even in a best case scenario of sustained emission limitations, there will be large stress on agri—food systems, infrastructure, ecosystems and human health. the union was an early actor on adaptation, with the adoption in 2013 of a strategy on adaptation to climate change. this aimed to enhance the preparedness and capacity of all governance levels to respond to the impacts of climate change and make europe more climate resilient. the new strategy will draw on its evaluation that was finalised in 2018 and, of course, will also take account of the european green deal ambitions. efforts to measure resilience to climate change need to continue and to be upgraded and linked to a more ambitious monitoring and evaluation system. the 2013 strategy relied on the scoreboard to assess preparedness. the revised strategy could use a dashboard to assess resilience and subsequently monitor its strength over time, with regular progress reports on specific targets. at the same time, strengthening effective monitoring and evaluation tools for adaptation policies and measures in partner countries will continue to be of central interest for the union’s international action and support. the commission’s proposal for a european climate law provides a framework for progress in pursuit of the global adaptation goal established in article 7 of the paris agreement. the adaptation strategy will be designed to support the achievement of the objectives of the proposal. the governance will include a citizens’ dimension through the recently—launched climate pact. the revised strategy will be accompanied by an impact assessment and will draw on the latest available research results. adaptation action in general, and the strategy in particular, will benefit from the increased climate—related spending target in the next union seven—year budget, while the european investment bank has committed in its recently—adopted climate roadmap to support its implementation. stakeholders will be empowered to tackle climate impacts like desertification and land degradation. climate change adaptation and disaster risk management will be a key priority for the european regional development fund and the cohesion fund in the 2021—2027 period, with a place—based approach to improving the resilience of eu regions and cities. today, the speed of adaptation actions varies across the union, with all member states having adopted national adaptation strategies or plans. in the eu member states, most vulnerability assessments are being made, and adaptations identified, in respect of agriculture, health, biodiversity, forestry, energy, oceans and seas. the european environment agency concludes that even if the union and some countries have started to monitor the implementation of adaptation activities, it’s not possible to determine with any certainty whether decisive progress in increased resilience at union level has been achieved by 2020. while building resilience and adapting to the impacts of climate change is a challenge for all regions of the world, it’s the poorest and most vulnerable who are least able to adapt, both with the union and globally, for example because of limited resources, protracted crises or violence. globally, the union and its member states remain the largest contributor of international public climate finance for adaptation purposes to developing countries, in particular least—developed countries and small island developing states. the union and its member states are committed to scaling up their financial assistance in the future. water resources, forests and agricultural crops fulfil many critical productive and regulation functions upon which our societies depend, such as clean drinking water, carbon sequestration, abundant food, wood and forest products, outdoor recreation opportunities and habitat. ensuring water, forests and agriculture can withstand a changing climate is critical to reaching essential goals, including preserving ecosystem services and not least the carbon sequestration potential of forests. the commission will take this issue up in all fora, including for cities in the global covenant of mayors. this issue is essential and the commission welcomes parliament’s early engagement and clear signal for ambition. we look forward to the upcoming parliamentary resolution on the new strategy and to engaging in fruitful discussion on implementation once the commission adopts the new strategy. but may i say that we also have to take care that the issue of implementation is properly addressed in the different sectoral legislation. the reports i have received so far are not very promising, at this stage at least.

the development of urban strategies that will include the use of the potential of all urban infrastructure, such as urban gardens, green roofs and sidewalks. i know we're all aware of how much climate change will affect our lives and our environment. i am particularly interested in cities because today more than two thirds of europe's population live in urban areas, or more than 350 million people, and this figure is growing. an increase in air temperature of more than 1.5 degrees celsius can cause the ground temperature to rise to more than 60 degrees. that's why it's so important to green these areas, whether it's rooftops, roads, or even glass buildings. i am sure that at this very moment in europe there are investment projects being co-financed by the european union, and i would this, as urban infrastructure can make a significant contribution to reducing the overall vulnerability of the union to climate change. to make a positive change, we must take into account many important environmental aspects. the investment plans of all member states and all areas that involve climate action, including research and development, must take account of our strategy. the been seeing on social media. they suggest that since there is abundant rainfall, resulting in floods and droughts, there is no drought or warming. ladies and gentlemen! if you ask a farmer if heavy rains irrigate crops, he will tell you that heavy rains do not provide enough water for the crops, because the water simply flows off the ground, often destroying the crops. i would therefore also like to draw particular attention to agriculture, which also faces many challenges in adapting to climate change. i would also like to call on all european local authorities to follow the example of european cities that have adopted local legislation to meet the european union's climate targets. achieving climate neutrality in terms of greenhouse gas emissions requires the active participation of both the government and local authorities, as well as all sectors of the economy and society as a whole. this will enable local authorities to be active partners for the industrial and construction sectors and, through the implementation of projects at local level, to actively support the implementation of the eu climate strategy. mother earth is responding to human activity, so all of us - regardless of the profession we represent - need to be aware of the seriousness of the problem and work together to prevent climate change.

madam president! the united kingdom left the european community, but it didn't leave europe. the united kingdom remains our neighbour, our ally and our economic partner. the establishment of a new relationship between the european union and the united kingdom is important not only because of the need for ongoing negotiations, but above all because of the need to maintain the unity of the west in an era of growing geopolitical challenges. the future relationship between the european union and the united kingdom must take into account the very strong economic ties, shared values and convergence of objectives in many areas. at the same time, they must ensure an appropriate balance of rights and obligations and take into account the political sensitivities of each party. strong economic links mean that greater ambition is needed, not only in terms of access to each other's markets but also in terms of ensuring a level playing field. the future agreement should ensure that new border control procedures are minimised while maintaining high security standards. this is particularly the case for agri-food commodities, which are particularly sensitive to border delays and regulatory issues. we need new solutions in transport: the vast majority of road transport in the european union and the united kingdom is operated by eu carriers. the agreement should provide for very ambitious solutions in this area, unprecedented in eu trade agreements. i would like to draw attention to the fact that, in addition to the economic dimension, cooperation in the field of internal security and justice must also be an important pillar of cooperation. the uk has left the european union, but the common threats remain. the exchange of data for the purpose of fighting crime, judicial cooperation in criminal matters, simplified extradition procedures and, finally, cooperation within europol all these elements should comprise a new partnership. threats such as fanatical islamic terrorism, human trafficking, drug trafficking, arms trafficking are still very real. brexit does not change anything here, and our cooperation to ensure the safety of our citizens
